sens: district of Israel established by Solomon
H0700.detail: Arubboth is a name of a region or district in Israel, established by King Solomon for administrative and tax purposes. This territory was associated with the collection of royal taxes. The district included the city of Soco and the land of Hepher, located in central Israel (1 Kings 4:10).
H0700.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "windows" (from the root עָרַב, "window"). The reason this territory received this name is not explained in the Bible; it may refer to a geographical feature of the place.
H0700.emploi: Arubboth is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:10, in a passage where Solomon divides his kingdom into administrative districts and appoints officials responsible for maintaining the royal court. This system of districts shows the complex organization of the Davidic-Solomonic government.

sens: man from Arabia or a region named Arab
H0701.detail: 1. This word refers to a man native to the region of Arabia or the locality called Arab (in the context of the Scriptures, it likely refers to a city in Israel). In 2 Samuel 23:35, Paaraï the Arab is mentioned among David's elite warriors, his thirty champions of war.
H0701.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְבִּי comes from the root עֲרָב (arab), which designates Arabia — this vast desert and region of the Middle East. The suffix -י (-i) indicates belonging to a people or place. This type of formation is common in Hebrew to identify men by their region of origin.
H0701.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Hebrew, in the catalog of David's warriors. It refers to Paaraï, one of the thirty champions who made up the king's military elite. Its isolated appearance in this context shows how Scripture honors men of valor from diverse regions, including Arab lands.
H0701.portee: This verse reminds us that strength and faithfulness to God knew no borders: David surrounded himself with the best warriors, wherever they came from. It illustrates how Scripture values loyal service in the Lord's service, regardless of origin or nationality.

sens: The whole number that follows three
The fourth rank or position in a series
The set of four elements or people
The number fourteen (in biblical dates of the Jewish calendar)
The number forty (archaic variant)
H0702.detail:
1. The number four simply designates the number that comes after three: the river of Eden divides into four branches (Genesis 2:10), animals have four legs according to the Law (Leviticus 11:20-23), and the cherubim each have four faces (Ezekiel 10:21).
2. The fourth element in a series: in genealogies, "the fourth generation" (Genesis 15:13), or the counts of the tribes listed by ranks (Numbers 2:4-9).
3. A group or set composed of four units: four cities assigned to the Levites (Joshua 21:35), four horns or four angels at the four corners of the earth (in biblical symbolism).
4. The number fourteen often designates the date of Passover: "the fourteenth day of the first month" (Leviticus 23:5; Ezra 6:19), which recalls the exodus from Egypt.
5. The number forty (rare in the provided texts) appears in composition: Jacob served Laban "forty years" (Genesis 31:41).
H0702.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְבַּע comes from an ancient root designating the number four. In Aramaic and in neighboring Semitic languages, the same word appears to express this number. The form of the word suggests an image of balance: four is the number of the sides of a square, the cardinal points, the legs of animals. In the Hebrew Bible, this number acquires strong symbolic resonances: the four rivers of paradise, the four horns and the four winds of heaven in prophecies, the four corners of the earth.
H0702.emploi: The word appears 277 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent numbers. It appears everywhere: in genealogies and enumerations (Genesis 11:13-17), in descriptions of the Tabernacle and its ritual objects (Exodus 25:12; 27:2-4), in the counts of the tribes of Israel (Numbers 1-2), and especially in cultic dates like Passover on the fourteenth day. Biblical writers also use it to describe natural phenomena (four legs of animals) and celestial visions (Ezekiel 10:21). Its basic meaning remains numerical, without positive or negative moral connotation.
H0702.portee: For the believer, the number four recalls the divine order of creation: four rivers water paradise, four animals appear in prophetic visions. It structures the habitable world (the four directions) and the cultic calendar (Passover on the fourteenth day marks God's salvation). It is a number of completeness and fulfillment.

sens: The number 4
H0703.detail: 1. The number four, which simply designates the quantity of 4 units. In Ezra 6:17, four hundred lambs are offered for the dedication of the temple. In Daniel 7:3, four great beasts come up from the sea. This is the most direct use of the word.
H0703.origine: This Aramaic word is borrowed from the biblical Hebrew אַרְבַּע (ar.ba), which means "four." It belongs to the same family as the number names in Semitic languages. The four was important in the Old Testament: the four cardinal points, the four horns of the altar, the four rivers of Paradise. Aramaic simply takes this ancient Hebrew word.
H0703.emploi: The word "four" appears six times in the Aramaic text of the book of Daniel and Ezra. In Ezra, it counts the victims of the sacrifice. In Daniel's visions (chapters 7 and 3), it takes on strong symbolic value: four winds, four terrible beasts coming up from the sea, four wings, four heads. In these prophetic passages, the number four often evokes the totality of earthly powers or the directions of the world, with a coloring of divine judgment. But the meaning remains primarily numerical.
H0703.portee: For the reader, the number four in these prophetic texts carries a spiritual weight. It marks the completeness of the reign of earthly empires in Daniel's vision, before the final judgment. It is a call to recognize that the history of the world will follow an order established by God, of which the number four is the seal.

sens: The whole number equal to four times ten
H0705.detail: 1. Forty is the number that results from four groups of ten units. It is a round number, frequently present in biblical narratives to express durations, quantities, ages, or counts. It appears in genealogical lists (Genesis 5:13, where Kenan lived forty years after the birth of Mahalalel), in the counts of the people (Numbers 1:21, which counts forty-six thousand five hundred men from the tribe of Reuben), or to mark the passage of time — like the forty years in the desert where God accompanied Israel (Deuteronomy 2:7: "The Lord your God has been with you for forty years"). This number recurs so often that it seems to express a complete period, a cycle marking the end of a trial or a generation, particularly in the narratives of the desert and divine judgments.
H0705.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְבָּעִים (arbaïm) comes from the root אַרְבַּע (arba), which simply means "four." By adding the suffix -ים (which marks the masculine plural), we get "the four" or "the four-tens" — that is, the number formed by the grouping of four tens. This number also appears in Aramaic and in neighboring Semitic languages.
H0705.emploi: The word forty appears more than a hundred times in the Hebrew Bible, in all historical and legislative books. It is used to count men in arms (Judges 12:14: Ibzan had forty sons), to mark durations of fasting or trial (Exodus 24:18: Moses remained forty days on Mount Sinai; Deuteronomy 9:9 and 9:18), to indicate ages or reigns (2 Samuel 5:4: David reigned forty years; 1 Kings 11:42: Solomon reigned forty years), or to set legal penalties (Deuteronomy 25:3: one cannot give more than forty lashes). In the context of the desert, forty years becomes a theological number marking the generation that must pass away before entering the promised land (Numbers 14:33-34; Numbers 32:13).
H0705.portee: The number forty, by its recurrence in key moments of salvation history, invites the reader to see in it more than a simple quantity: it is a number of judgment and transformation. When Israel goes through forty years in the desert, it is not an arbitrary duration, but the time that God sets to purify His people and prepare them for their inheritance. This number reminds us that God controls the time and seasons of life, and that His trials always have a limit and a purpose. Recognizing the theological significance of forty helps to read Scripture with an awareness of the divine intentions hidden behind the numbers.

sens: Numerical multiplier that expresses a quantity repeated four times
Restitution at quadruple for a stolen or damaged item
H0706.detail:
1. This word is a form of the number four that indicates a repetition or multiplication by four. It literally means "four times" or "the quadruple."

2. In the judicial and restitution context, it designates the payment of four times the value of a good: it is a severe penalty imposed on one who has committed theft or damage. In 2 Samuel 12:6, the prophet Nathan condemns King David to return four sheep for taking Naboth's only sheep, which expresses both the serious guilt and the required restitution.
H0706.origine: The word comes from the Aramaic and Hebrew root "four" (arba), augmented by the suffix "-ayim" which marks the double or multiplication. This grammatical form transforms the simple cardinal number into a multiplier. The notion of quadruple appears in biblical law as an enhanced punishment for certain offenses.
H0706.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 12:6. It is found in the context of the parable that Nathan addresses to David to denounce his sin with Bathsheba: the prophet describes a rich man who stole a poor man's only sheep, and establishes that the thief must return four sheep. This judicial and symbolic language serves to make David understand the gravity of his act and the extent of the restitution he should make.
H0706.portee: This passage reveals that biblical law does not settle for equal restitution: it imposes an increased penalty to punish theft or damage, particularly when it affects the weak. For the believer, this shows that sin, especially that committed by a leader against the vulnerable, entails increased guilt and requires restitution commensurate with the injustice and lack of compassion.

sens: Interlace threads to form a fabric
Braid or intertwine hair
One who weaves, artisan of weaving
To use cunning or scheming
H0707.detail:
1. To weave means to interlace threads of warp and weft to create a fabric. It is the work of the weaver with his loom. The Bible speaks of woven garments, such as the high priest's tunic in Exodus 39:27, where the artisans make tunics of fine linen "woven."
2. The verb also applies to braiding or intertwining hair: Samson falls asleep on Delilah's knees, who weaves his hair in Judges 16:13-14, thus attaching it to the loom.
3. By extension, the word designates the weaver himself, the artisan who weaves: in 1 Samuel 17:7, Goliath's spear has a shaft "like a weaver's beam," that is, the rod on which the warp is wound.
4. Figuratively, to weave can mean to scheme, to prepare in secret. In Isaiah 38:12, the prophet says that God "will finish me" like a weaver who "cuts me off from his loom," an image of human life as a weaving that God completes or cuts.
H0707.origine: The Hebrew verb אָרַג comes from a root that expresses the idea of interlacing, of creating by interlacing. The same root produces the noun "weaver" (one who weaves). The basic image is that of the loom where the threads interlace: it is an ancient and universal human gesture, fundamental for the making of clothing and fabrics.
H0707.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the context of textile craftsmanship and sometimes of scheming. In the literal and concrete sense, it describes the work of weavers who make the garments for worship (Exodus 28:32; 39:27), or the braiding of hair (Judges 16:13-14). The spear of giants is compared to a "weaver's beam" (1 Samuel 17:7; 1 Chronicles 20:5), which shows the massive size of the shaft. Isaiah uses the image of weaving to speak of fragile human life: it is like a fabric that the weaver cuts (Isaiah 38:12), or of malice that weaves plots (Isaiah 59:5).
H0707.portee: This word reminds us that manual work — here weaving — is a true and worthy art in the eyes of God. The garments of the high priest, woven with care, are part of the holiness of worship. The image of weaving to describe human life (Isaiah 38:12) invites the reader to see their life as an ongoing weaving, where each day adds a thread, and only God knows the end. It is a meditation on the fragility and brevity of earthly life.

sens: moving rod of the loom that passes the thread from one end to the other
the resulting thread, that is, the fabric
figuratively, the rapid passage of time and life
H0708.detail:
1. It is the part of the loom that moves quickly to interlace the threads: it goes back and forth from right to left. In Judges 16:14, when Samson is asleep, Delilah "fastens the hair of his head to the loom's peg" — this indicates how well-known and functional this shuttle is.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the fabric itself that is created through this shuttle work.
3. Figuratively, Job uses the image of this constantly flying shuttle to evoke the rapidity of a life that passes: "My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle" — a poignant comparison to express how brief and fleeting human existence is.
H0708.origine: The Hebrew word אֶרֶג (erev) literally refers to the shuttle or the loom. It comes from a root that evokes interlacing and weaving. It is a technical term from craftsmanship, well attested in the vocabulary of the ancient Near East for traditional looms.
H0708.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In the dramatic context of Judges 16:14, it refers to Delilah's loom — the narrative relies on it for its realism: Samson's hair is attached to the shuttle itself. In Job 7:6, it takes on its poetic and metaphorical dimension, where the rapid movement of the shuttle becomes an image of the brevity of life and the fleeting nature of time.
H0708.portee: This word reminds us that Scripture speaks of concrete and ordinary realities — work, crafts — to help us understand great truths. Job's image especially confronts us with the fleeting nature of our existence and should prompt us to reflect on the value and brevity of our days.

sens: region of Bashan known for its fortified cities
eastern territory conquered by Israel
region allotted to the tribe of Manasseh
H0709G.detail:
1. Argob is a region of Bashan, east of the Jordan, famous for its many fortified cities surrounded by walls and bronze bars (1 Kings 4:13). It is an important and prosperous territory, strategically well defended.
2. At the end of the conquest, Moses and Israel take possession of all the cities of Argob, which was part of the kingdom of the giant Og (Deuteronomy 3:4). This region, given to the Israelites as war booty, has about sixty large cities.
3. Moses allocates Argob to the half-tribe of Manasseh as an inheritance (Deuteronomy 3:13), which will become the domain of the judge and warrior Jair, son of Manasseh; the towns of Argob will bear his name: the towns of Jair (Deuteronomy 3:14).
H0709G.origine: The Hebrew name Argob literally means "heap of clods" or "rocky and uneven terrain." The region is named for its rocky and steep terrain, characteristic of the topography of Bashan. It is a descriptive term for the landscape that designates this plateau with a high density of fortifications.
H0709G.emploi: Argob appears four times in the Bible, always referring to this same eastern region. It is mentioned during the account of the conquest of Bashan by Moses (Deuteronomy 3:4, 13, 14) as a key territory, and again in the time of Solomon, in the administrative context of his royal officials (1 Kings 4:13). The region retains its strategic and economic importance throughout Israel's history.
H0709G.portee: This region illustrates how God keeps His promises: He gives Israel well-fortified and prosperous lands, which become stable possessions for the tribes. The name Argob reminds us that God's blessing is not solely about wealth, but about defended lands where the people can live in safety.

sens: officer of King Pekah of Israel
H0709H.detail: Argob is an officer who serves King Pekah during the period when the kingdom of Israel is divided in two. He participates, along with another officer named Ahijah, in the conspiracy that overthrows King Pekahiah: together, they strike him dead in the royal palace of Samaria, allowing Pekah to take power (2 Kings 15:25).
H0709H.origine: The name Argob literally means "heap of clods" or "mass of earth," an image of something solid and massive. This name is also borne in the Old Testament by a mountainous region of Bashan, which may explain the choice of this name for an officer: something stable, fundamental. Here, it simply designates a man, a servant of the king.
H0709H.emploi: Argob appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 15:25. He is presented as an officer of the royal house of Israel, one of the two conspirators who assassinate King Pekahiah in Samaria. Alongside Ahijah, he plays a prominent role in this coup d'état, after which Pekah ascends to the throne.

sens: reddish-purple color obtained by dyeing
fabric or garment dyed this color
royal or priestly luxury and wealth
H0710.detail:
1. Purple is a reddish-purple color, very expensive to obtain in antiquity. It was extracted from marine shells and required a long dyeing process, making it extremely valuable.
2. The word also refers to the fabric itself, dyed purple: it was a luxury cloth reserved for kings and high priests. In 2 Chronicles 2:7, Solomon requests a craftsman capable of working with "purple-dyed fabrics," showing that only the greatest royal works required it.
3. By extension, purple symbolizes wealth, power, and dignity: wearing purple was a display of royal or priestly status. This is why it appears among the noblest fabrics intended for the Temple.
H0710.origine: The Hebrew word argouvan is borrowed from Phoenician or Akkadian, the commercial languages of the peoples who controlled the production of this dye in the Mediterranean. Its Aramaic equivalent (אַרְגְּוָן) is practically identical, indicating that the word traveled with commerce itself. The root evokes the idea of a bright and brilliant color.
H0710.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (2 Chronicles 2:7), but this passage says a lot: it is included in the list of noble materials that Solomon requests for building the Temple in Jerusalem. This unique mention increases its significance: purple is a marker of absolute luxury, attested throughout the ancient Near East as the color of royal and priestly power.
H0710.portee: For the Christian reader, purple evokes dignity and power. The New Testament mentions it especially in the Passion, where it becomes the ironic symbol of the soldiers' mockery of Jesus. Here, in 2 Chronicles, it recalls the glory of Solomon's Temple and Davidic kingship as a reflection of God's splendor.

sens: Fabric or garment of red-violet color
Insignia of dignity and royal or princely power
H0711.detail:
1. Purple is a fabric dyed in a rare and precious red-violet color in antiquity. It was obtained from a natural dye derived from shellfish. In Daniel 5:7, the king promises the wise man who interprets the mysterious inscription that he "will be clothed in purple" — it is a sumptuous garment reserved for high-ranking individuals.
2. To clothe someone in purple means to entrust them with a prominent position and to give them the insignia of their authority. When Daniel receives this robe (Daniel 5:29), it is also a gold chain and the promise of a high office in the government. Purple then symbolizes power, nobility, and honor.
H0711.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew אַרְגְּוָן (ar.ge.van), attested as early as the Old Testament to denote this prestigious dye. Its exact origin remains debated, but it reflects the ancient trade of purple, well known to the Phoenicians. The word traveled with the empires and languages of the Mediterranean.
H0711.emploi: The word appears only three times in Aramaic, in the book of Daniel in chapter 5. King Nebuchadnezzar (Belshazzar) offers it as a reward to anyone who can decipher the mysterious writing on the palace wall. Daniel, after reading and explaining the inscription, is indeed clothed in purple (Daniel 5:7, 5:16, 5:29). Each occurrence emphasizes the importance of this honor: first as a promise, then as a reaffirmation of the promise, and finally as fulfillment. Purple marks the exceptional and exceptional recognition.
H0711.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage illustrates how God elevates His faithful servants and honors them before the powers of the world. Daniel receives the purple not by calculation or ambition, but because he has been faithful to God and divine wisdom. It is a reminder that true dignity comes from integrity and dependence on God, rather than the pursuit of earthly honors.

sens: Closed container, made of wood or metal, intended to hold and transport objects
Box containing offerings or precious goods
H0712.detail:
1. A chest is a solid, closed container designed to protect and transport what is placed inside. It is an everyday object, like a box or a crate. In 1 Samuel 6:8, a chest is placed next to the ark of God on the cart to protect it during transport.
2. By extension, this chest can be a special container intended to receive valuable items or offerings: in 1 Samuel 6:8 and 6:15, the chest contains the gold objects that the Philistines give to the Lord in compensation for their sin, namely the mice and the gold tumors shaped as votive images.
H0712.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְגַּז (argaz) literally means a box or chest, probably of foreign origin or borrowed, as suggested by its characteristic form. It is encountered exclusively in the account of 1 Samuel 6, when the Philistines return the captured ark to the Israelites. This particular term emphasizes the precise and historical nature of the account: it is the technical word for the box that accompanies the ark.
H0712.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, solely in 1 Samuel 6:8, 6:11, and 6:15. All uses occur in the episode where the Philistines return the ark to the Israelites after capturing it. The chest accompanies the ark on the cart and contains the compensatory offerings in gold — the mice and the figures of the tumors — that the Philistines offer to seek God's forgiveness. The context is one of religious restitution and atonement.
H0712.portee: This chest reminds the reader that even in times of misfortune or conflict, God protects what belongs to Him. The Philistines recognize the power of the Lord and seek to repair their guilt by placing the signs of their atonement in a chest accompanying the ark — an act of restitution and submission to divine will.

sens: Red-violet or blue-violet color obtained by dyeing
Fabric or garment dyed in this color
Sign of wealth, dignity, and royal power
H0713.detail: 1. Purple is a rich color, between red and violet, obtained by dyeing textile fibers. It is a precious and brilliant hue that requires particular craftsmanship: skilled women of Israel spun linen and other fibers "dyed in blue, purple, and scarlet" (Exodus 35:25), alongside other noble colors. 2. The word also refers to the fabric itself once dyed, used to make garments of great prestige. The ephod of the high priest, the quintessential sacred garment, was made "of gold, blue thread, purple and scarlet, and fine twisted linen" (Exodus 28:6), or the curtains of the Tabernacle, finely embroidered. 3. Purple thus becomes the symbol of royal power and supreme dignity: it adorns kings, princes, and authority figures. In Babylon, skilled artisans worked it to embellish royal garments and thrones (Ezekiel 27:7, 27:16), and it marked those who bore eminent authority.
H0713.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְגָּמָן (argaman) likely comes from an ancient Semitic root meaning dye. Purple was extracted from marine shellfish (particularly the murex), making production extremely costly and rare in antiquity. In Greek, the word πορφύρα (porphyra) translates this Hebrew term, and both refer to the same prestigious dyeing practice of the Levant and the Mediterranean world. The rarity of the dye and the complexity of the process made purple a royal commodity.
H0713.emploi: The word purple appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Exodus (description of the Tabernacle and its priestly garments) and sporadically in other books. In Exodus, purple is one of the three prestigious colors (along with blue and scarlet) required for the Tabernacle, the high priest's garment, and the curtains: it is a noble and regulated liturgical material. Outside the Tabernacle, it adorns royal palaces (Esther 1:6, with cords of fine linen and purple), the garments of kings and princes (Esther 8:15), and it figures in the precious goods of Phoenician and Babylonian trade (Ezekiel 27:7). The word gradually enriches: from simple dye (Exodus 25), it becomes an emblem of status and wealth.
H0713.portee: For the Christian reader, purple reminds us that God has consecrated the finest materials and the most beautiful craftsmanship for the worship rendered to Him. It also evokes, in the New Testament, the mockery of Christ clothed in purple before His passion — a moment when earthly authority mocks the King of kings. Purple teaches us that true dignity does not reside in external adornment, but in the consecration of the heart.

sens: Son of Benjamin, mentioned during the descent into Egypt
H0714G.detail: 1. Ard is a son of Benjamin, the youngest of Jacob's twelve sons. He appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:21, when Jacob and all his family descend into Egypt to join Joseph. His name is listed among the ten sons of Benjamin at that time.
H0714G.origine: The name Ard literally means "I will subjugate" or "I will tame" in Hebrew, formed from a root evoking domination or mastery. It is a typical name from ancient Semitic times, borne by this member of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of Moses.
H0714G.emploi: Ard is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:21, in the genealogical list of Benjamin's sons. He appears alongside his nine brothers (Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ahiram) at the time when Jacob descends into Egypt with his entire family. This enumeration marks the establishment of the tribe of Benjamin in the land of Egypt during the stay before the Exodus.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela
Ancestor of a family of Israel
H0714H.detail:
1. Ard is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Bela, who lived at the time of the Exodus and in the wilderness. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the census of Israel in Numbers 26:40, where he is listed among the descendants of Bela along with his brother Naaman.
2. Because of him, a family lineage called "the Ardites" was born, meaning the descendants of Ard. This family name appears at the time of the second census of the people at the threshold of the Promised Land, thus showing Ard's genealogical importance in the history of Israel.
H0714H.origine: The name Ard means "I will subdue" in Hebrew, expressing an idea of domination or mastery. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries a spiritual intention. His descendants are called "Ardites" (Hebrew: ardî), which specifically designates those who belong to his family lineage.
H0714H.emploi: Ard appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:40, during the census of the tribes of Israel in the wilderness. He is presented as the son of Bela and brother of Naaman, Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, Iri, Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, and Ahoah — that is, a member of the well-documented genealogical Benjaminite branch. Although mentioned only once, his existence and descent are deemed significant enough to be recorded in the official genealogies of the chosen people.
H0714H.portee: Ard reminds us that the Bible honors even the minor figures in the history of Israel by recording their names and lineage. For the reader, this shows that God knows each of His people, even those who are mentioned only once, and that every human life is part of the story of salvation.

sens: Son of Caleb and Jerioth, man of the tribe of Judah
H0715.detail: Ardon is a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Caleb and the woman Jerioth. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Caleb in 1 Chronicles 2:18, where he is named among the children that Caleb had with Azubah, his wife, and Jerioth. Although he is not well known, he belongs to the important lineage of Caleb, the tribal leader who accompanied Moses and Joshua in the conquest of Canaan.
H0715.origine: The name Ardon means "he who subdues" or "fugitive," composed of a Hebrew root expressing the idea of domination or flight. This name reflects a valued quality or an event in the life of the one who received it. The family of Ardon, that of Caleb, is one of the great houses of Judah, whose descendants play an important role in the history of Israel.
H0715.emploi: Ardon is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 2:18. He appears in the genealogical list of Caleb's children, alongside his brothers Jesher and Shobab, who were born to Azubah. This genealogy continues with other children of Caleb born to other women, testifying to the importance of Caleb's house in the tribe of Judah and the necessity of preserving the memory of the generations who inherited the Promised Land.

sens: member of the clan of the descendants of Ard
H0716.detail: 1. The Ardites are the descendants of Ard, a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived at the time of the Exodus and in the wilderness. This term designates the individuals who belonged to this family group and who, like the other clans of Israel, were counted during the censuses of the people in the wilderness (Numbers 26:40).
H0716.origine: The name "Ardite" comes from Ard, which itself means "I will subdue." Ard was one of the sons of Bela, who was himself a son of Benjamin. Family names of this type, formed by adding the suffix "-ite," are common in the Old Testament to designate clans and their descendants.
H0716.emploi: The term "Ardites" appears only once in the Bible, during the second census of the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers 26:40). It is included in the list of families of Benjamin, recorded for the civil and military organization of God's people. Ard is presented as one of the three sons of Bela along with Naaman and several other brothers: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, Iri, Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, and Ahoah.

sens: To pluck a plant, fruit, or flower to harvest it
To gather or collect what grows
To strip someone of their belongings
H0717.detail:
1. The literal meaning of the verb is to pluck or gather what grows: grapes from a vine, fruits from a tree, flowers from a garden. It is a concrete act of harvest. In Song of Solomon 5:1, the beloved "gathers" myrrh and spices from the garden, as one collects the fragrant treasures of the earth.
2. By extension, the verb can refer to the act of gathering, collecting a harvest or crop as a whole. It carries the idea of stripping or stealing what belongs to someone else.
3. In Psalms 80:13, the word expresses the idea that passersby strip the vine: they "gather" or ravage it, meaning they pillage its riches without right, making its wealth disappear.
H0717.origine: The Hebrew verb אָרָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of tearing away or removing. The word belongs to the family of action verbs: to gather, to remove, to take. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this verb is often rendered by the Greek τρυγάω (trugaô), which also means "to harvest grapes" or "to gather the vintage." The initial image is that of the hand grasping and tearing away what grows.
H0717.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Song of Solomon 5:1, it describes the concrete act of the beloved gathering the perfumes from his garden, an act of intimacy and enjoyment. In Psalms 80:13, it appears in a very different context: the vine planted by God has its fences "broken," so that "all passersby strip it" or "gather it." Here, the verb takes on a nuance of violence and loss: what was protection becomes an occasion for theft. The context determines whether the action is an act of joyful harvest or a form of pillaging.
H0717.portee: This word reminds the reader that every harvest, every enjoyment of what God has given, depends on divine protection and blessing. When the vine is exposed and stripped, it is not just a material loss: it is a sign of the withdrawal of God's guard. Conversely, being able to freely gather what the garden produces is an image of peace, communion, and satisfaction in God.

sens: Call to attention: ‘look’, ‘pay attention’
Announcement of an appearance or an event that suddenly arises
Affirmation of the reality of what has just been said
H0718.detail:
1. This word serves to draw the reader's or listener's attention to something that suddenly appears or is important to notice. In Daniel 7:2, Daniel says, ‘here, the four winds of heaven broke forth’: he signals to the reader a crucial event he has just seen in vision.
2. It announces the visible and sudden appearance of something or someone: in Daniel 7:5, 7:6, 7:7, ‘here’ introduces a new beast that appears in the night vision each time, reinforcing the impression of an unexpected and spectacular appearance.
3. It affirms that what follows is real and worthy of faith, especially in prophetic visions. In Daniel 7:13, ‘here’ prepares for the appearance of the Son of Man, giving prophetic weight to the revelation.
H0718.origine: This Aramaic word (the section of Daniel in the Old Testament is written in Aramaic) comes from the same family as the Hebrew ‘alalé’ (אַלְלַי, ‘alas!’), which also expresses an interjection. It is an interjection, meaning a word that is exclaimed rather than declined, and serves to punctuate speech rather than describe.
H0718.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only in the book of Daniel, specifically in 7:2, 7:5, 7:6, 7:7, and 7:13 — always in the prophetic visions of chapter 7. Each time, Daniel reports what he has seen ‘during his night visions’ and uses ‘here’ to mark the sudden arrival of a creature or new figure. The word emphasizes the immediacy and visual strength of the revelation: these are not reported stories, but events of which Daniel is a witness and shares urgently with his reader. It is a word of prophetic reporting.
H0718.portee: This word invites the reader to share in the seer's experience: he is not passive, he is invited to ‘look’ with Daniel at what is happening in the heavens. For a Christian, this reminds us that prophecy is never abstract, but always tied to visions, images, a reality that God shows. Understanding this movement of attention (‘look!’) helps to enter into prophetic consciousness and to receive God's message not as a theory, but as a personal call.

sens: Phoenician city-island near Sidon
its inhabitants, the Arvadites
H0719.detail: Arvad is a fortified island located on the Phoenician coast, not far from Sidon. It was famous for its sailors and experienced warriors. The text of Ezekiel 27 mentions it twice in its lament over Tyre: first in 27:8, where the inhabitants of Arvad are among the most skilled rowers serving the merchant city of Tyre, alongside the experts from Sidon; then in 27:11, where the Arvadite warriors and their valiant men lined the walls and towers of Tyre, hanging their shields everywhere to reinforce the defense. These two passages show that Arvad was a leading maritime and military center in the ancient Phoenician world.
H0719.origine: The name etymologically means ‘I will break’ or ‘I will be free’, an image likely related to its insular position. Arvad belonged to the prosperous Phoenician cities of the Levant coast, and its inhabitants were known throughout the Mediterranean basin for their skills in navigation and combat.
H0719.emploi: Arvad appears only twice in the Bible, in verses 8 and 11 of Ezekiel 27, both in the long prophetic lament over the fall of Tyre. This lament lists the peoples and cities that had commercial and military relations with Tyre at the height of its splendor. Arvad is mentioned alongside Sidon as one of the major Phoenician partners: it provided expert rowers and renowned warriors. This mention underscores the strategic and economic importance of Arvad in the Phoenician network.

sens: Son of Gad and chief of a family in the tribes of Israel
H0720.detail: Arod is one of the sons of Gad mentioned at the time of the census of the Israelites in the desert. He gives his name to a family, the Arodites, which is encountered in the census of the people at the foot of Sinai (Numbers 26:17).
H0720.origine: The name Arod literally means ‘I will submit’ or ‘I will wander’, formed from a Hebrew root evoking either domination or running and movement. It is a typical name of the patriarchs and ancestors of the tribes of Israel, bearers of God's promises.
H0720.emploi: Arod appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:17, during the second census of Israel in the desert after the exodus from Egypt. He is presented as one of the seven sons of Gad, who gave birth to the family of the Arodites. His name appears in the official genealogies of the chosen people, marking his place in the history of Israel and the tribal heritage passed down to future generations.

sens: Merchant people of the Phoenician coast, descendants of Canaan
Inhabitants of the city of Arvad, ancient port of the eastern Mediterranean
H0721.detail: 1. The Arvadians are a Canaanite people established on the Mediterranean coast, recognizable among other Canaanite peoples such as the Sidonians, Jebusites, or Amorites (Genesis 10:18). They form a branch of the larger family of Canaanites, descendants of Canaan himself. 2. Arvad is an important port city on the Phoenician coast, and the Arvadians are its inhabitants and merchants. Like Sidon, mentioned alongside them, it is an active maritime center of antiquity.
H0721.origine: The name comes from Arvad, a Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast (present-day Ruad, an island in Syria). Arvad literally means ‘I will break’ or ‘I will escape’, perhaps evoking the island that emerges from the waves or a city easily accessible by sea. The demonym ‘Arvadians’ simply designates the people originating from this city, just as ‘Sidonians’ refers to the inhabitants of Sidon.
H0721.emploi: The Arvadians appear twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in the genealogical lists of Genesis 10 and its parallel in 1 Chronicles 1, which enumerate the Canaanite peoples. They are listed alongside other coastal and land peoples of Canaan, forming the context of the ancient Mediterranean world. The Bible mentions this nation without recounting any specific interaction with Israel, unlike other Canaanite peoples.
H0721.portee: This mention reminds the reader that the world in which the history of Israel unfolds was not isolated, but surrounded by organized and trading peoples. The Arvadians embody the earlier or contemporary Canaanite civilizations, forming the backdrop of God's plan for Canaan. Their enumeration underscores the scope and diversity of the nations that God knew and whose destiny He guided.

sens: Son of Gad and ancestor of a tribe of Israel
Member of the family of the Arodites
H0722.detail: Arodi is the name of one of the twelve sons of Gad, one of the twelve sons of Jacob who each became the head of a tribe of Israel. His name appears in the list of the sons of Gad during the descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:16). Later, the people descended from him bear the collective name of ‘Arodites’ to designate the family or clan formed by all his descendants (Numbers 26:17).
H0722.origine: The name Arodi is the patronymic form of the name Arod, which literally means ‘one who descends from Arod’. Its Hebrew root evokes the idea of ‘to submit’ or ‘to roam’ (hence the double meaning ‘I will submit’ and ‘I will roam’). This type of name, formed from the name of the father or ancestor, was common in Israel to designate clans or tribal families.
H0722.emploi: Arodi appears twice in the Bible, at two key moments of the census of Israel. First in Genesis 46:16, he is listed among the sons of Gad who descend with Jacob into Egypt during the famine. Then, in Numbers 26:17, during the second census in the desert, after the exodus from Egypt, the same ancestor is mentioned, but this time in reference to his descendants organized into the clan of the ‘Arodites’. These two mentions mark the genealogical continuity between Egypt and the desert, and the establishment of the twelve tribes of Israel.

sens: Jebusite who lived during the time of the united kingdom of Israel
owner of a threshing floor near Jerusalem
man who sold his land to King David to build an altar
H0728.detail: Aravna is a Jebusite (inhabitant of Jebus, the ancient name of Jerusalem) who appears during a dramatic event: a plague strikes the people of Israel as a result of David's sin of taking a census. At that moment, the angel of the Lord stops to destroy above Jerusalem, right near the threshing floor (the space for grain threshing) that Aravna owned (2 Samuel 24:16). The prophet Gad then commands David to go up to this land to build an altar to the Lord (2 Samuel 24:18). Aravna, recognizing the king coming to him with his entourage, humbly bows down and generously offers not only his threshing floor but also his oxen and wood so that David can make the sacrifice that will appease divine anger (2 Samuel 24:20-23). This land will later become the site of Solomon's temple, the spiritual heart of Israel.
H0728.origine: The name Aravna (אֲרַוְנָה) literally means "shout of joy of Jah" or "I will shout for joy," expressing gladness. It is sometimes spelled Ornan (אׇרְנָן) in other passages. The name reflects optimism and trust in God, even though its bearer is a non-Israelite (a Jebusite).
H0728.emploi: Aravna appears exclusively in the account of 2 Samuel 24, during the plague that follows the census of the people. He is mentioned seven times, always in relation to his threshing floor and his encounter with David. Three key passages show his evolution: first, as a simple owner of the land where the angel destroys (2 Samuel 24:16), then as the seller whom David seeks to compensate (2 Samuel 24:18 and 24:21), and finally as the generous man who refuses payment and offers everything for free (2 Samuel 24:22-23). His character, progressively revealed, makes him a model of reverence towards the God of Israel, despite his foreign origin.
H0728.portee: Aravna illustrates how God uses men of all backgrounds to accomplish His plans of redemption. His act of giving his property so that David could build an altar shows the power of true repentance and reconciliation: the cursed land becomes holy. His selfless generosity—refusing payment and giving goods and livestock—depicts the reverent respect inspired by true divine worship, beyond the boundaries of race or nationality.

sens: To transport and bring to a place
To present or lead before someone
H0729.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to physically transport something from one place to another, then to bring it to its destination. In Ezekiel 27:24, the goods—precious fabrics and cedar chests—are "brought" to the markets of Tyre, meaning they are transported and presented for sale.
2. More broadly, "to bring" can mean to lead or present someone or something before a person or in a place: it conveys the idea of an arrival that makes present and visible.
H0729.origine: The Hebrew verb ʾāraz comes from a root that expresses the idea of solidity, firmness. The meaning of "to bring" derives indirectly from this: what is "brought" with assurance, firmly transported, arrives safely. The word belongs to a semantic field where the strength and certainty of the act of transporting give meaning to the verb.
H0729.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 27:24. It is part of a poem about the wealth and commerce of Tyre, listing the goods that peoples brought to this prosperous trading city. The mercantile context and the parallel with goods "tied with ropes" and "made of cedar wood" emphasize the idea of organized and reliable transport of precious goods.
H0729.portee: This verb reminds us that in the Bible, even the details of commerce and transport reflect the order of the world created by God. The enumeration of goods brought to Tyre highlights both human prosperity and its vanity: all this wealth is destined to fall according to the prophecy of Ezekiel.

sens: majestic tree of Lebanon with precious wood
cedar wood used in construction
cedar wood used in purification rites
symbol of strength, grandeur, and durability
H0730.detail:
1. The cedar is a large tree from Lebanon, known for its majestic size and high-quality wood, highly valued in antiquity. Psalms 92:13 compares the righteous who flourish to a cedar of Lebanon, an image of strength and elevation.
2. Cedar wood was highly prized for the construction of important buildings in Israel. Thus, the temple of Solomon and his royal palaces featured columns, beams, and panels of cedar (1 Kings 7:2, 1 Kings 6:9), showcasing the wealth and splendor of the king.
3. In terms of purification, cedar played a role in the rites of the law. Leviticus 14:4 commands the use of cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop to purify someone who has been healed of leprosy: cedar represented purity and restoration.
4. Cedar symbolizes greatness, strength, and permanence. In prophetic passages, the destruction of the cedars of Lebanon represents divine judgment on the powerful (Isaiah 2:13, Ezekiel 31:3).
H0730.origine: The Hebrew word אֶרֶז comes from an ancient Semitic root designating this characteristic tree of Lebanon. The cedar of Lebanon was a prestigious species throughout the ancient Near East, symbolizing magnificence and solidity. This word does not change in different contexts of the Bible: it always refers to the same tree or its wood.
H0730.emploi: This word appears 69 times in the Bible, mainly in the historical books (1 and 2 Kings, 1 and 2 Chronicles) that describe the construction of the temple and royal palaces. It is also found in the psalms (where it illustrates the strength of the righteous), in the prophets (where it symbolizes earthly powers judged by God), and in the laws of purification (Leviticus and Numbers). The context varies: sometimes it is the tree itself growing on the mountains of Lebanon (Psalms 29:5), sometimes it is the wood used to build royal buildings or the temple (1 Kings 5:6-10), and sometimes it is a biblical symbol of strength and grandeur (Psalms 92:13, Ezekiel 31:3).
H0730.portee: The cedar teaches the reader several spiritual truths. First, that God provides for the splendor and solidity of the works dedicated to Him, like the temple built with the finest wood. Second, that earthly greatness—even that of majestically planted cedars—is subject to God's judgment and can be cut down. Finally, that the righteous who roots himself in God grows with the strength of a cedar of Lebanon (Psalms 92:13), an image of spiritual stability and lasting growth.

sens: Noble wood of cedar, known for its durability and fragrance
Panel or wainscoting made of cedar used to decorate buildings
Wealth and splendor of a place, symbol of power
H0731.detail:
1. Cedar is a precious wood, known since antiquity for its exceptional strength and pleasant scent. This wood is used in grand royal and sacred constructions, notably to adorn the interior walls and wainscoting of palaces (Zephaniah 2:14).
2. The word here refers to the panels or wall coverings made from this noble wood. These cedar wainscoting adorned important buildings and marked the splendor of a residence. When Zephaniah announces that "the cedar wainscoting will be torn down" from the city of Nineveh, he describes the complete destruction and humiliation of this powerful city.
3. By extension, cedar symbolizes the wealth, solidity, and beauty of a construction. The loss of these noble wainscoting signifies the total ruin of the past glory of a stronghold.
H0731.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְזָה (arzah) comes from the root אָרַז (araz, "cedar"), which designates the majestic cedar tree of Lebanon. This wood was highly prized in the Ancient Near East for the construction of temples and royal palaces, particularly in Egypt and Mesopotamia.
H0731.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zephaniah 2:14, where it describes the cedar wainscoting that adorned the city of Nineveh. This prophetic passage announces that even the most luxurious and durable finishes will be destroyed during the judgment on this great Assyrian city. The use of cedar here symbolizes not only material wealth but underscores the extent of the devastation to come.
H0731.portee: The mention of cedar reminds us that even the most solid and prestigious works of man, built on injustice, do not withstand the judgment of God. This poetic detail invites the reader not to place their trust in earthly splendor but to fear the Lord who brings down the mighty.

sens: One who makes a journey, who moves from one place to another
One who passes by, transient, without settling
To travel a road, to walk
To associate with someone, to walk together
Meal given to a traveler, hospitality
To know, to be aware (very rare sense)
H0732.detail:
1. A traveler is someone who moves, who goes from one place to another — this is the most basic sense of the word. The old man in Judges 19:17 sees this man traveling, who has come from afar.

2. The traveler is primarily one who is passing through: he does not live there, he crosses the land for a night, a few days. He is a temporary stranger, like the one described in Jeremiah 14:8, "a traveler who enters to spend the night."

3. The verb also means to walk, to traverse a path — it is the action of the journey itself. When it is said that one "walks" in the company of those who do evil (Job 34:8), it means walking alongside them on the same path.

4. To associate, to walk with someone: this meaning derives from the previous one — to walk together means to share the same journey, to accept the same direction.

5. A traveler's meal (2 Samuel 12:4): the food prepared to welcome the one who travels, the hospitality offered to the passerby.

6. Rarely, the word takes on the meaning of knowing or being aware (Psalms 139:3: "you know when I walk") — a very particular usage, perhaps related to the idea of knowing through experience, through the path traveled.
H0732.origine: The Hebrew root ארח (arach) refers to the primary idea of a path, a way — the track one follows, the road one takes. It is linked to the image of a person who moves, who follows a direction. The word has generated several forms: the traveler (noun), to travel or to walk (verb), to walk together, to take a path. The central image remains that of movement, of progression on a path.
H0732.emploi: The word appears six times in the Bible. It is primarily a noun: the traveler, a figure of the passerby, the temporary stranger, a foreigner who can be received or overlooked (Judges 19:17, Jeremiah 9:2, Jeremiah 14:8). It is also used for the hospitality offered to the traveler, the "meal" prepared for him (2 Samuel 12:4). As a verb, "to travel" or "to walk" refers to both the simple action of moving (Psalms 139:3) and walking in company with someone, with a moral nuance: to walk with the wicked means to share their path and their choices (Job 34:8). The rare sense of "to know" in Psalms 139:3 shows that knowing can be expressed through the idea of walking — God knows our paths because He walks them with us, and nothing escapes His sight on our journey.
H0732.portee: This word reminds us that life is a path, a journey: we are only passing through this earth, "temporary travelers." It raises the question of hospitality towards those who pass by — a central virtue in the ancient East and in Israel. It also poses the moral question: with whom do you walk? Will your companions lead you towards good or evil? Finally, when God "knows" our paths, it is the assurance that no action, no step of our life escapes Him: He walks alongside us.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher
Son of Ulla
H0733G.detail: Arach is a man of the tribe of Asher mentioned in the genealogical account of 1 Chronicles 7. He appears as the son of Ulla, alongside his brothers Hanniel and Ritsja (1 Chronicles 7:39), in the list of descendants of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy.
H0733G.origine: The name Arach means "traveler" or "one who travels," evoking the idea of a journey or a path. It is a simple Hebrew name, borne by several men in the Bible: members of families from Judah and Asher, as well as family leaders among the exiles who returned from Babylon.
H0733G.emploi: Arach is a proper name designating a man from Asher, a family father, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 7:39 in a genealogy of the clans of Asher. This mention is part of the genealogical lists that structure the book of Chronicles, preserving the memory of the tribal lineages of Israel. The same name has been borne by other men in the history of Israel, notably among the family leaders upon their return from exile, but this entry specifically concerns the son of Ulla.

sens: Family leader among the exiles who returned from Babylon
H0733H.detail: Arach is the name of a man who led an important family during the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. He appears in the lists of those who returned to Jerusalem: in Ezra 2:5, there are seven hundred seventy-five sons of Arach among the repatriates; in Nehemiah 7:10, this number is six hundred fifty-two. His name designates both the man himself and the family clan that descended from him, significant enough to be recorded in writing as an identified group in the eyes of the return authorities.
H0733H.origine: The name Arach means "traveler" in Hebrew, an image that suits this man well: he led his large family on the long and difficult journey back from exile, crossing the desert to regain the promised land. It is a meaningful name that evokes both movement and perseverance necessary to accomplish this march.
H0733H.emploi: Arach is mentioned twice in the Bible, both in the official lists of repatriates during the return from exile in the fifth century B.C. In Ezra 2:5 and Nehemiah 7:10, these two nearly identical passages — which preserve the trace of administrative records — register the clans that returned from captivity under the leadership of Zerubbabel. The slight difference in numbers (775 then 652 sons) may reflect counts at different times or an alternative tally. These lists show that important families played a key role in the restoration of Israel after the exile.

sens: Jewish man from the time of exile and return
Head of a family among the returning exiles
Member of the tribe of Asher
H0733I.detail:
1. Arach is a man's name found in the Bible at the time of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. The context of Nehemiah 6:18 shows him as a figure with significant family ties in Jerusalem, whose name appears in the genealogies of the return.
2. He is presented as the head of a family of returning exiles, meaning those who return to the Holy Land after the exile. His social weight or prestige is highlighted by the fact that several Judeans are "bound to him by oath" (Nehemiah 6:18), suggesting either a marital alliance or a relationship of influence or protection.
3. The Hebrew indicates that Arach was a member of the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He thus represents a genealogical continuity with the pre-exilic past.
H0733I.origine: The name Arach literally means "traveler" or "one who travels" in Hebrew. This etymology evokes the image of a person on a journey, which fits perfectly for a man of the return from exile: after decades in captivity in Babylon, Arach and his descendants make the long journey back to Jerusalem. The name therefore reflects his historical condition as a repatriate.
H0733I.emploi: Arach appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 6:18. This passage, located in the book of Nehemiah which recounts the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the return from exile (circa 445 B.C.), mentions Arach as the father of Shecaniah. The text emphasizes his alliance ties with other influential Judean families: several Judeans are bound to him by oath, and his descendants unite with those of Meshullam, son of Berechiah, showing the social importance of his family among the repatriates.

sens: a path traveled on foot or horseback
the course, the direction of a person's life
the way of living, moral conduct
the moral or spiritual behavior of a people or a person considered as just or unjust
H0734.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a way, a physical path taken to go from one place to another. A path is generally narrower and less traveled than a road (Proverbs 15:19: "the path of the sluggard is like a hedge of thorns").
2. Figuratively, it represents the journey, the trajectory of human life, what happens to someone over the course of their days. It is the image of a traveler who progresses, encounters obstacles or traps (Psalms 142:4: "you know my path. On the road where I walk they have laid a trap for me").
3. The path also describes the way of living, the habits and moral choices of a person (Proverbs 4:18: "the path of the righteous is like the shining light").
4. Finally, it designates the overall moral or religious orientation of a person or a people: the righteous walk on the right path, the wicked on a twisted path (Proverbs 2:15: "their paths are crooked"). God "teaches his paths" (Psalms 25:4), which means he guides man toward a righteous life.
H0734.origine: The Hebrew word עורח (ōrach) comes from a root that means "to go, to move." It is related to other words denoting travel or walking. It is a natural and everyday image: in the biblical world, most movements were made on foot or horseback on paths. This concrete image of the way has become one of the richest in biblical religious language to describe spiritual life.
H0734.emploi: The word appears 57 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms (18 occurrences) and Proverbs (17 occurrences), which explore moral and spiritual life. It is also found in historical narratives and among the prophets. Its uses vary according to the context. Among the sages (Proverbs), the path is constantly evaluated: some lead to life, others to death, folly, or traps. In the Psalms, it is often God who "knows," "teaches," or "keeps" the paths of the one who prays. Among the prophets (Isaiah, Micah), God's paths become an invitation to repentance: man must change paths and follow divine will.
H0734.portee: This word invites the reader to see their life as a conscious journey, a path to choose. It reminds that every act, every decision directs the course of one's existence. For the believer, it is especially God who illuminates the path: Psalms 25:4 expresses this fundamental request to be guided. The path is not a place where one glides passively, but a way one takes, where one stands up, where one deviates or perseveres. It is a call to responsibility and trust in the one who knows our way better than we do.

sens: Path or road taken
Way of acting, conduct, line of life
H0735.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a path or a physical way that one travels. But in the text of Daniel, it takes on a figurative meaning: the "ways" of God are not earthly roads, but his manner of acting and governing. In Daniel 4:37, Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges that "all the works" of God and his "ways" are just — he speaks of God's justice in all that he does.
2. The word also means the entirety of a person's conduct, their line of life. In Daniel 5:23, God "holds in his hand your breath and all your ways": he controls not only the king's vital breath but also his entire path, all his actions and decisions. It is the idea that the whole life of a man, from his choices to his destiny, is in God's hands.
H0735.origine: This Aramaic word is very close to its Hebrew equivalent (אֹרַח, ôrach, #H0734). It comes from a root evoking the idea of walking or moving. The same word appears in other Aramaic texts and in biblical Hebrew with the same fundamental meaning: a path, a way, a direction.
H0735.emploi: The word appears only twice in Aramaic in the Bible, both in the book of Daniel. In Daniel 4:37, King Nebuchadnezzar uses it to speak of the justice of God's "ways" — his manner of governing the world is right and true. In Daniel 5:23, the word describes the "ways" of King Belshazzar, meaning all his actions and way of life. In these two passages, "way" never designates a simple path, but rather the conduct, behavior, or manner of acting of a person or of God.
H0735.portee: This word reminds the reader that God sees and controls not only our major decisions but also the entire trajectory of our life. It also invites reflection on God's justice: his "ways" are never unjust or twisted. For the believer, this means that trusting in God's direction is to recognize that he leads with justice and wisdom.

sens: Group of merchants or travelers moving together
Convoy of camels or pack animals transporting goods
Organized commercial expedition across the desert
H0736.detail:
1. A caravan is a group of people traveling together, usually for trade or safety reasons. In the story of Joseph, Jacob's sons see a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead and heading to Egypt, carrying precious spices (Genesis 37:25): this is an organized trading expedition.
2. The word also more specifically refers to the convoy itself with its pack animals. The camels heavily laden with spices, balm, and myrrh form the heart of this caravan: they are the strength of the journey.
3. This is a typical way of traveling in the ancient Near East: gathering several merchants, several pack animals, and traveling in a group to mutually protect against the dangers of the desert and bandits. In Isaiah 21:13, the caravans of Dedan are addressed as passersby of the desert, showing that these convoys are common and recognizable phenomena.
H0736.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to journey" or "to travel": the idea is one of organized movement. It is related to a verb that describes the action of setting out. It is a concrete word, drawn from the daily life of the Near East, where commercial travel across deserts required group organization to survive.
H0736.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It is used each time to describe a group of merchants in motion: in Genesis 37:25 for the Ishmaelite caravan that buys Joseph, and in Isaiah 21:13 for the caravans of Dedan crossing the Arabian desert. It is a word specific to the context of ancient commercial travel, without particular religious nuance, but loaded with biblical imagery of exchange and destiny.
H0736.portee: This word anchors the Bible in historical and geographical reality: it speaks of real journeys, real markets, the actual economy of the ancient world. For the believer, the caravan in Genesis 37 reminds us how God uses ordinary events—even the slave trade—to fulfill His plan. It is an invitation to see divine providence in the details of the world around us.

sens: What is given to someone for living: food, clothing, money
Regular allowance intended to cover daily needs
Grass, fodder for animals
H0737.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to what is provided to someone to ensure their material survival. In 2 Kings 25:30, the king of Babylon continually provides for the daily maintenance of a royal prisoner: this means he gives him daily sustenance, food, and perhaps clothing. It is an act of regular and reliable support.
2. The word can also refer to the allocation itself, the ration assigned. Jeremiah 52:34 speaks of daily maintenance: it is the portion of food or allowance that someone receives each day, consistently and measured.
3. It also applies to what nourishes animals: in Proverbs 15:17, grass (simple food for the poor) is contrasted with a fattened calf (refined dish). Grass here is the ordinary, humble but sufficient nourishment.
H0737.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to arrange" or "to dispose." It evokes the idea of a regularly organized and distributed allocation: something planned, stable, that ensures order and continuity. It is a word from the domain of stewardship and resource management.
H0737.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Old Testament, mostly in contexts of dependence or assistance: twice in relation to the king of Babylon providing for the maintenance of a captive king (2 Kings 25:30 and Jeremiah 52:34, parallel accounts), once in Jeremiah 40:5 where the chief of the guards gives provisions to someone leaving prison, and once in Proverbs 15:17 where grass becomes a symbol of simple and honest food. The word emphasizes the regular, dependent, and assured nature of what is provided: the one receiving maintenance is not solely responsible for their survival.
H0737.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on dependence and providence. The one receiving maintenance acknowledges their need and vulnerability: they depend on others. For the Christian, this can evoke dependence on God and trust in His daily provision (as in Matthew 6:11, "the bread for today"). The proverb about grass also reminds us that peace and love in the home are worth more than material abundance.

sens: Fierce animal with a mane, formidable carnivore of the ancient Near East
Sculpted or engraved representation of a lion, ornament or decoration
Strength, power, and dominance
Ferocity, threatening violence
Martial courage and bravery in battle
H0738A.detail:
1. The lion is a large wild animal that inhabits the territory of Israel and the ancient Near East. It is a powerful and dangerous predator: Samson tears one apart with his bare hands (Judges 14:5), and David also has to face lions while guarding his sheep (1 Samuel 17:34). Benaiah fights several, including one in a snowy pit (1 Chronicles 11:22).
2. Because of its impressive strength, the lion becomes a decorative motif: lions are carved on the royal throne (1 Kings 10:19) or on the panels of the temple supports (1 Kings 7:36), to remind of royal majesty and dominance.
3. The Bible uses the lion as an image of irresistible power: Israel rises "like a lion" (Numbers 23:24), meaning with a strength that nothing stops until its victory. God Himself can roar like a lion (Isaiah 38:13).
4. The lion also represents brutal and threatening menace: a wicked person dominating a poor people is "like a roaring lion and a hungry bear" (Proverbs 28:15). It is destructive ferocity, ruthless oppression.
5. For warriors, the lion symbolizes indomitable martial courage: David and his companions are "strong as lions" (2 Samuel 1:23) in battle.
H0738A.origine: The word אֲרִי (arî) is the classical Hebrew term for lion in the Near East. It comes from an ancient root common to Semitic languages, evoking the beast that roars and devours. The physical power of the lion has made it, early on, a symbol of royalty, divine power, and dominance throughout the region. Lions indeed roamed the Promised Land during biblical times, although they disappeared after antiquity.
H0738A.emploi: The word appears 33 times in the Old Testament, first in narratives (Numbers, Judges, Samuel) where it refers to real lions faced by heroes. The wisdom books (Proverbs) use it in moral and pedagogical comparisons: the lazy invents obstacles ("a lion is in the street," Proverbs 22:13). The word is also used to describe royal and sacred ornaments (Kings, Chronicles). The prophets use it to depict divine power or the threat of judgment: Jeremiah and Ezekiel employ it to show God or enemies in their fearsome strength. In lyrical poetry (Song of Songs), the lion evokes the majesty of the beloved.
H0738A.portee: The lion reminds us that God possesses absolute strength, peaceful for the faithful believer but terrifying for the enemy. It invites the reader to contemplate not weakness or fear, but the power of the Lord: the one who believes does not fear, because more powerful than any lion is He who created them all. It is also a lesson in vigilance: the figurative lion warns us against the threat of evil, which prowls like a predator.

sens: Fearsome carnivorous animal of the Mediterranean region and the Middle East
Powerful and courageous warrior or king
Evil creature that devours or lurks
Image of divine strength and God's judgment
Symbol of messianic peace when transformed
H0738B.detail:
1. The lion is a wild animal, feared for its strength and devastating jaws. Judah is compared to "a young lion" that lies down after the carnage (Genesis 49:9), an image of a powerful beast at rest.

2. A powerful king or warrior is called "lion" for his bravery and boldness: the people fear a leader as one fears a leaping lion (2 Samuel 17:10).

3. The lion also symbolizes the danger that lurks and devours: David prays to escape from those who "tear me apart like a lion" (Psalms 7:3), or from one who "lies in wait like a lion" (Psalms 10:9).

4. God himself roars "like a lion" to warn (Hosea 11:10, Amos 3:8) or His judgment strikes "like a lion" (Jeremiah 50:44): the image suggests the irresistible power of the Lord.

5. In the vision of messianic peace, the lion becomes harmless and peaceful: it "will eat straw like the ox" (Isaiah 65:25), a symbol of universal transformation when the Messiah reigns.
H0738B.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְיֵה (aryeh) simply refers to the lion, a well-known animal in the Near East. It is a common term that does not derive from a more complex ancient root, but it directly evokes the creature itself by onomatopoeia or by ancient designation. In Aramaic, the word exists in the same form and carries the same meaning. This term appears in many proper names: Ariel ("lion of God"), Ari ("my lion"), combinations that show the prestige of this animal in the biblical imagination.
H0738B.emploi: The word "lion" appears about 40 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetic and prophetic texts. Genesis 49:9 opens a long series of royal comparisons: Judah is a lion, a symbol of his dominance. In history, the lion can be a real danger (1 Kings 13:24-28), but more often it is an image: of sin that devours (Jeremiah 2:30), of a fearsome enemy (Jeremiah 4:7, Jeremiah 5:6), or of the strength of God Himself. The prophets use it to describe divine judgment (Jeremiah 50:44, Amos 3:8). Finally, messianic visions transform it: from terror, the lion becomes a peaceful companion in the future reign (Isaiah 65:25).
H0738B.portee: The lion shows the biblical reader that brute strength is not enough to truly reign: only one who possesses divine power — or who depends on it — can govern sustainably, like Judah. The lion that prowls and devours also warns of the danger of sin that lurks like a predator. Finally, the image of the lion transformed into a gentle creature calls for hope: only God can reconcile the world and reshape hearts, ending the carnage to establish His peace.

sens: Elite warrior of King David
H0739.detail: Ariel is the name of a military leader who is among the "mighty men" of King David, during the time when Israel was strong and unified under his reign. He is mentioned as having accomplished remarkable feats in battle.
H0739.origine: The name Ariel literally means "lion of God" in Hebrew (from "ari", lion, and "el", God). It is a name that evokes the strength and pride of the king of beasts, bearing divine power — an appropriate image for a renowned warrior.
H0739.emploi: Ariel is mentioned twice in the Bible, always in connection with David's army. In 2 Samuel 23:20, he is presented among the "mighty men" (the heroes of David), and the same passage is repeated in 1 Chronicles 11:22 in the parallel list of military exploits. These two mentions complement each other to testify to his prominent role in the royal army of the First Temple.

sens: Leader of the exiles returned from Babylon
Poetic nickname for Jerusalem
H0740G.detail:
1. Ariel is a Jewish leader who participated in the return of the exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem during the time of the governor Ezra. He is among the leaders that Ezra summons to organize the journey (Ezra 8:16).
2. The name Ariel literally means "lion of God". This nickname has been applied to Jerusalem itself, probably to evoke its strength and majesty, like a lioness protecting the holy city.
H0740G.origine: The Hebrew name consists of two elements: "ari", which means "lion" (the king of beasts, symbol of strength and power), and "El", the divine name "God". Ariel thus means "lion of God" or "lioness of God". This type of name composed with "El" was common among the Hebrews to express a special relationship with God.
H0740G.emploi: Ariel appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:16. It is a personal name, that of a leader or official whom the priest Ezra designates to prepare for the return of the exiles from Babylon. This mention underscores the importance of this man in organizing the return of the Jewish people to Jerusalem, without providing further details about his life or actions.

sens: Jerusalem, the holy city where King David dwelled
H0740H.detail: 1. Ariel is a poetic and symbolic name for Jerusalem. The name means "lion of God" or "lioness of God", evoking the divine strength and majesty that protect the city. This title emphasizes the sacred bond between God and His city, the one that David established as the capital of his kingdom (Isaiah 29:1).
H0740H.origine: The word Ariel combines two Hebrew words: "ari" (lion) and "El" (God). It is a symbolic and poetic name created to express the special relationship between God and Jerusalem — God is seen as the powerful lion who watches over the city. This type of descriptive name was common in biblical poetry to amplify the spiritual meaning of a reality.
H0740H.emploi: Ariel appears three times in the Bible, only in the prophet Isaiah in chapter 29, in a prophetic passage announcing the siege of Jerusalem. Isaiah uses this symbolic name to speak of God's judgment on the city and what will follow. The prophet uses the same word twice in verses 1-2 to emphasize the importance of the divine message, and a third time in verse 7 to refer to the nations that will fight against it. The context is one of affliction and prophetic punishment.
H0740H.portee: This name reminds us that Jerusalem is not just a political capital, but the city of the "lion of God", marked by divine intervention. For the believer, it evokes the majesty and protection of God over His people, even in times of trial and judgment.

sens: The sacred structure where offerings and sacrifices are burned
The upper or central part of this structure, where the fire is maintained
Metaphorically, the place of encounter with God through sacrifice
H0741.detail: 1. The altar is the stone or wooden construction erected in the Temple or sanctuary where the priests perform the sacrifices: it is where the victims and offerings are burned for the Lord. Ezekiel 43:15 and 43:16 precisely describe its dimensions (four cubits high, twelve cubits long and wide) and its four horns, which are ornamental but also symbolic protrusions marking the four corners. 2. The word particularly designates the hearth or firebox, the upper part where the wood and sacrifices blaze: it is the ardent heart where the smoke rises to heaven. 3. Beyond the material object, the altar represents the point of contact between the people and God: it is the visible sign that man can approach the Lord through sacrifice and obtain His forgiveness.
H0741.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of strength or fire. Its etymological link refers to the notion of a blazing hearth or structure of power, which fits well with a place where the fire of God consumes the offerings. The word is connected to the theology of sacrifice in the Old Testament: the altar is the instrument by which guilt is atoned for and communion with the Eternal is restored.
H0741.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Ezekiel 43, where the prophet receives a detailed vision of the future Temple and its altar. In these two consecutive verses, Ezekiel scrupulously describes the structure: first the horns marking the four corners (43:15), then the complete dimensions making it a square of twelve cubits (43:16). These very precise descriptions reflect the theological and liturgical importance of this altar in the Temple worship: it is a monumental, fixed, and regular altar, contrasting with the nomadic altars or high places of earlier periods.
H0741.portee: The altar reminds the reader that God has instituted a concrete and orderly means for man to come to Him and find forgiveness: it is not a vague or spiritual relationship, but visible and tangible. For a believer of the New Testament, the Temple altar represented the work of Christ, who offers Himself as the ultimate sacrifice. Contemplating the altar is to recognize that the restoration of the relationship with God comes through a self-giving and acceptance of divine judgment.

sens: Son of Haman, killed during the vengeance of the Jews
H0742.detail: Aridai is one of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian vizier who sought to destroy the Jews during the reign of Ahasuerus. When Haman's plot is discovered and he is hanged, the king allows the Jews to defend themselves. During this retaliation, Aridai and his nine brothers are killed in Susa, the capital (Esther 9:9).
H0742.origine: The name Aridai means "the lion is enough" or "the lion suffices" in Hebrew. It carries the idea of strength and authority, like a dominating lion. It is a typically Persian name from the time of ancient Middle Eastern history, borne in the family of the great enemy of the Jews.
H0742.emploi: Aridai is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 9:9, where his name appears in the list of the ten sons of Haman executed on the same day. This precise enumeration shows the extent of divine revenge: not only is Haman himself punished, but all his male descendants are annihilated, preventing his house from perpetuating its hatred against the Jews.

sens: Son of Haman, listed among his ten sons
H0743.detail: Aridatha is one of the ten sons of Haman, the enemy of the Jews during the reign of Ahasuerus. His name appears in the list of Haman's sons killed during the vengeance of the Jews in Susa, an event recounted in chapter 9 of the book of Esther.
H0743.origine: The name Aridatha means "the lion of the decree." It belongs to a group of proper names of Persian origin that characterize the atmosphere of the book of Esther, written during the time of the captivity and the return of the Jews.
H0743.emploi: Aridatha is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Esther 9:8, in the enumeration of the ten sons of Haman.
