This enumeration carries symbolic importance in the narrative: it confirms that the vengeance of the Jews reached all the heirs of the plot against the chosen people, thus fulfilling the reversal of fate that the Jews had risked suffering.

sens: fearsome wild animal, carnivorous with a mane
powerful and fierce creature
instrument of royal and divine punishment
image of strength and danger
H0744.detail:
1. The lion is a large carnivorous animal, a symbol of power and ferocity in the ancient Near East. In Daniel 6:7, the kingdom's officials propose that anyone who prays to another god be thrown "into the lions' den": this is one of the most terrible royal punishments, where the man becomes prey.
2. The ferocity of the lion is fearsome: it is feared for its violence. Yet, in Daniel 6:22, the angel of God "shuts the mouths of the lions," and Daniel emerges unharmed from the den (Daniel 6:20). It is the lion presented as a force that can only be tamed by divine power.
3. The lion here becomes an instrument of royal power: the Persian king uses the lions' den as an extreme punishment for those who disobey his edict. Thus, it is a figure of judgment and death.
H0744.origine: The Aramaic word אַרְיֵה comes from the same root as the Hebrew word אַרְיֵה (see H0738B). It is a simple word that directly designates this fearsome animal of the Levant. The image is that of an untamed wild beast, a universal symbol of brute strength and deadly danger.
H0744.emploi: The word appears nine times in Aramaic in the book of Daniel, exclusively in chapter 6 (verses 7, 12, 16, 19, 20, 22, 24, 27) and once in chapter 7 (verse 4). All these uses concern the lions' den where King Darius orders Daniel to be thrown. The context is political and legal: it is a royal punishment. In Daniel 6:22, the word takes on a spiritual dimension when the angel shuts the mouths of the lions, revealing that only the living God can master what seems invincible.
H0744.portee: The story of Daniel in the lions' den shows that the brute power of the world — symbolized by this fearsome predator — has no power over one who trusts in God. This passage encourages the believer not to fear earthly threats when their faithfulness to God is unwavering.

sens: Officer of King Pekahiah of Israel
H0745.detail: Arié is an officer who served King Pekahiah of Israel during the time of the divided kingdoms. His name means "lion" in Hebrew. He participated, along with Pekah and Argob, in the conspiracy that led to the assassination of Pekahiah and the usurpation of the throne by Pekah around 740 BC (2 Kings 15:25).
H0745.origine: The name Arié comes from the Hebrew root aryeh (אריה), which means "lion." It is a name that evokes strength and power, common in ancient Israel to express vigor and warrior courage. The same word designates the animal in other biblical passages.
H0745.emploi: Arié is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 15:25. He appears among the conspirators who assassinate King Pekahiah of Samaria. The Segond calls him "Arié"; he is associated with Pekah and Argob in this bloody coup that marks a turning point in the history of the Northern Kingdom.

sens: ancient king of Ellasar, ally of Kedorlaomer
H0746A.detail: Arjoc is a king of ancient Near East mentioned twice in the account of Genesis 14. He reigns over Ellasar and allies with Kedorlaomer, king of Elam, as well as two other kings (Amraphel and Tidal) to wage war against the five kings of the Pentapolis (including the king of Sodom). This Arjoc participates in the battle where Lot, Abraham's nephew, is captured, prompting Abraham to intervene to rescue him.
H0746A.origine: The name Arjoc comes from a Semitic root meaning "lion": the name evokes the idea of strength, of a powerful royalty. He is a king of the ancient world, likely contemporary with the patriarch Abraham, whose story fits into the context of wars between kingdoms of Mesopotamia and the Levant.
H0746A.emploi: Arjoc appears only in Genesis 14, the account where Abraham intervenes militarily to save Lot. He is named twice: first in verse 1 as "king of Ellasar" alongside Kedorlaomer and the other allied monarchs, and then in verse 9 when the author again lists the four kings against the five. There is no other mention of this character in the Bible. His role is that of a military ally in a coalition to conquer the lands of the Jordan.

sens: Chief of the guards of King Nebuchadnezzar
Officer responsible for executing the wise men of Babylon
H0746B.detail: Arjoc is an officer of the Babylonian court, chief of the guards (or executioners) of King Nebuchadnezzar. He is the one who receives the king's order to execute all the wise men of Babylon, including Jewish captives like Daniel, when no one can interpret the royal dream (Daniel 2:14). Daniel approaches him with caution and wisdom to persuade him to grant a delay before the execution. Arjoc agrees to bring the young Hebrew before the king, showing some kindness or at least an openness to negotiation (Daniel 2:24-25). Thus, he becomes the instrument through which Daniel can be presented to the sovereign and have his request granted.
H0746B.origine: The name means "lion-like," an image of power and strength. Arjoc is a historical figure of the Babylonian court, mentioned only in the book of Daniel. His name reflects the context of the Babylonian empire and the authoritative role he held.
H0746B.emploi: Arjoc appears four times in the book of Daniel, only in chapter 2. He is presented as the chief of the guards or executioners of King Nebuchadnezzar, responsible for executing the wise men of Babylon who cannot interpret the king's dream. Daniel meets him diplomatically and respectfully and manages to convince him to give him a delay and present him to the king. Arjoc plays a crucial transitional role: he is the intermediary between Daniel and Nebuchadnezzar, allowing the young Hebrew to manifest his divine wisdom.
H0746B.portee: The figure of Arjoc illustrates how wisdom and prudence can sway even those who hold power and authority. Daniel does not resist by force, but by intelligence and respect; Arjoc, although an officer of a powerful king, shows himself capable of listening and acting with mercy. It is a reminder that divine Providence can use those around us, even in the most perilous circumstances, to accomplish its purposes.

sens: Son of Haman mentioned in the account of the Jews' vengeance under King Ahasuerus
H0747.detail: Arizaï is one of the ten sons of Haman. He is mentioned only in Esther 9:9, in the list of Haman's sons who were killed by the Jews during the days of vengeance authorized by King Ahasuerus. His name does not appear anywhere else in the Scriptures: he is a strictly secondary character, known only through this genealogy of the tyrant who sought to destroy the entire Jewish people. Along with his brothers, he embodies the descendants of the one who stood against the people of God.
H0747.origine: The Hebrew name אֲרִיסַי (Arizaï) would mean "lion of my banners" or a similar expression, although the exact meaning remains obscure. Like all the names of Haman's sons, it carries a characteristic Persian resonance, which fits the context of the narrative since Haman was a dignitary of the Persian court. The names of Haman's sons reflect the splendor and power claimed by this arrogant character.
H0747.emploi: Arizaï appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 9:9, where he is listed among the ten sons of Haman killed on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. The complete enumeration of names seeks to show the extent of the Jews' vengeance and the divine judgment that struck even the descendants of the one who plotted their extermination. This mention alongside his nine brothers constitutes all the biblical information we have about this character.

sens: To extend in duration, to last long
To make something last, to extend it in time
To continue to live, to survive
To extend in space, to become longer
H0748.detail:
1. To extend in duration: the word first describes something that persists, that lasts a long time. When Isaac "prolongs" his stay with Abimelech (Genesis 26:8), he stays there for a long time, to the point that the king notices him. Similarly, in Ecclesiastes 8:12, a sinner who "perseveres long" in evil sees his days stretch out.
2. To make last, to extend: this is the voluntary action of maintaining something. God commands the people to "prolong their days" by obeying His commandments (Deuteronomy 4:40 and 22:7): to obey is to live long. Isaiah is instructed to "prolong" the cords of his tent, meaning to make them longer (Isaiah 54:2).
3. To continue to live, to survive: in Judges 2:7, the elders who "survived" Joshua are those whose lives were prolonged after his death. It is the persistence of the vital breath.
4. To extend in space: the word can also describe what stretches physically. In Psalms 129:3, plowmen have "traced" long furrows in the back of the psalmist: the furrows are long, prolonged.
H0748.origine: The Hebrew verb אָרַךְ comes from a root that expresses the idea of length, both in time and space. The basic image is that of something that extends, that lengthens. The word is used in the simple (Qal) to describe what is or becomes long, and in the causative (Hiphil) for the action of making long, of prolonging. This root is found in late Aramaic with the meaning of "to suit, to be appropriate": by prolonging something, one makes it fit for its purpose.
H0748.emploi: The verb appears 34 times in the Old Testament, especially in Deuteronomy, in the Psalms, and among the Prophets. Its most frequent usage concerns the prolongation of life: obeying God prolongs days, as reiterated in Deuteronomy (4:40, 5:16, 22:7). It is a driving force of ethical behavior in the Torah. It is also applied to the duration of a stay (Genesis 26:8), to perseverance in evil (Ecclesiastes 8:12), to concrete realities such as tent cords (Isaiah 54:2) or furrows (Psalms 129:3). In Numbers 9:19 and 9:22, it describes how the people remain camped under the cloud for a long time. The word radiates especially a promise: to obey is to live.
H0748.portee: This verb opens to the believer a major biblical reality: long life is not a matter of chance, but the fruit of obedience and the fear of God. It reminds us that our time is in the hands of the Lord and that our moral choices have concrete consequences on our existence. Conversely, the pursuit of evil "prolongs" the days of the sinner without giving him peace (Ecclesiastes 8:12–13). It is an invitation to cherish life by walking in God's ways.

sens: That which is appropriate, fitting for the situation
That which is just, timely, worthy of being done
H0749.detail:
1. The word describes what is suitable and timely, what truly fits the moment and circumstances. In Ezra 4:14, the king's officers say that it does not seem "suitable" to them to see the king despised: they mean that it would be inappropriate, contrary to what is right to do towards a sovereign.
2. The idea includes a notion of moral appropriateness or decorum: what is "suitable" is what imposes itself as just and correct in a given relationship or situation.
H0749.origine: The word comes from the Aramaic root corresponding to the Hebrew אָרַךְ (arakha), which fundamentally means "to be long" or "to extend." From there, the meaning of "to be in agreement with," "to suit" has developed — what extends well, what adjusts, is what is appropriate. It is an Aramaic word, as it appears in the Aramaic portion of the book of Ezra.
H0749.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament in Aramaic (Ezra 4:14). It is used by the Persian officers of the king to express their concern: it does not "seem suitable" to them to allow the king to be insulted. The context shows that it is about evaluating what is appropriate, just, and worthy in a relationship of honor towards royal authority.
H0749.portee: This word reminds Christians that they are called to discern what is "suitable" — what aligns with their faith, with the respect due to God and those around them. It is an invitation to wisdom and decorum in our actions and words.

sens: Who takes time to become angry, who restrains their anger
Who acts without haste, with patience
Who requires time, who lasts long
H0750.detail:
1. A heart slow to anger is a heart that does not ignite immediately when offended: it takes time for rage to rise. That is why the Lord is described as "slow to anger" in Exodus 34:6, not because He does not hate sin, but because He restrains His judgment and gives time for repentance. A man slow to anger shows wisdom, for "he who is slow to anger has great understanding" (Proverbs 14:29).
2. Slowness can also mean patience in the face of trials or restraint in the face of provocations. In Ecclesiastes 7:8, slowness to anger calms disputes: it cuts through with restraint rather than force.
3. The word can denote something that extends over time or takes a long time to manifest: a slow anger is an anger that comes gradually, unlike a sudden outburst.
H0750.origine: The Hebrew word אָרֵךְ comes from a root that means "long," "extended." It primarily describes duration or distance. When applied to anger, it paints it as something that stretches, taking time to reach its boiling point. That is why Nahum 1:3 says that God is "slow to anger": even in the face of evil, He does not react with an immediate strike but allows time to act.
H0750.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Hebrew Bible. It primarily describes God Himself: it is one of the major qualities of God's character (Exodus 34:6, Psalms 103:8, Nehemiah 9:17). The phrase "merciful and compassionate God, slow to anger" recurs as a refrain reminding the people of their Creator's infinite patience. The word also describes a moral virtue in man: the wise person is slow to anger (Proverbs 14:29, 16:32), while he who is quick to anger proclaims his folly. In Jeremiah 15:15, the prophet begs God to be slow to anger towards his persecutors, revealing how believers view this slowness as a form of grace and protection.
H0750.portee: For the believer, discovering that God is slow to anger is a comfort: even when we sin, we are not immediately destroyed, but the Lord gives us time to repent. And for those who believe in Christ, this divine slowness reveals God's patience towards all men, including His enemies. In return, the wise cultivate the same virtue: to be slow to anger is to imitate God and receive His discernment.

sens: ancient city of Mesopotamia
H0751.detail: Erech is an important city of ancient Mesopotamia, located about 64 kilometers northwest of Ur, on the left bank of the Euphrates, towards Babylon. It appears in Genesis as one of the first cities that Nimrod established in his power, at the origins of human civilization after the Flood.
H0751.origine: The name comes from a Hebrew root meaning "long"; the city itself was known in antiquity by the Akkadian name Uruk (corresponding to the Hebrew Erech). It was one of the oldest Sumerian cities, founded several millennia before our era.
H0751.emploi: Erech appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 10:10, where it is mentioned among the cities that King Nimrod established in the land of Shinar (Lower Mesopotamia). It symbolizes the cradle of the first urban human civilizations, before the time of Abraham. Modern archaeologists have confirmed that Uruk-Erech was indeed one of the largest cities of the ancient world.

sens: That extends considerably in time
That has a great extent, a large measure in space
That lasts, that persists (speaking of a situation)
H0752.detail:
1. That extends considerably in time: the word describes a duration that does not end quickly. In 2 Samuel 3:1, "the war lasted a long time" expresses that the conflict prolonged over a considerable period, threatening the outcome of the confrontation.
2. That has a great extent, a large measure in space: Job 11:9 speaks of the wisdom of God whose "measure is longer than the earth," meaning that its extent, depth surpasses even the dimensions of what we can spatially conceive.
3. That lasts, that persists (speaking of a situation): in Jeremiah 29:28, the message announces "it will be long, the captivity," meaning that the exile to Babylon will extend over a long period, a duration for which the exiles must prepare to bear the weight.
H0752.origine: The Hebrew word arkh comes from a root that evokes the idea of something that stretches, extends. It is related to other Hebrew words expressing length and extension in time or space. The fundamental image is that of something that does not stop short, that continues, that fills a large space or a long duration.
H0752.emploi: The word appears three times in the transmitted Hebrew Bible through the available usages. It first applies to the duration of a war (2 Samuel 3:1), then to the immeasurable spatial extension of divine wisdom (Job 11:9), and finally to the predictable length of an exile (Jeremiah 29:28). Its usage thus focuses on the idea of an extension — temporal or spatial — that is remarkable, difficult to bear, or hard to measure. In each context, "long" introduces a notion of challenge or greatness.
H0752.portee: This word invites the reader to take the measure of what God allows or what He is. When the war lasts a long time, it reinforces the stakes of the conflict and political instability. When God's wisdom proves longer than the earth, it is an invitation to humility before the infinity of His understanding. When captivity is announced as long, it is a call to patience and trust in God despite prolonged trial.

sens: Dimension that extends in the direction of the elongation of an object
Duration, extent of a period of time
Patience, self-control, ability to endure without reacting
H0753.detail:
1. Length is the measure that goes from one end to the other of an elongated object. It is the major dimension, the one that is measured first when describing a building or a piece of furniture. Genesis 6:15 gives the example of the ark: "three hundred cubits in length," and 1 Kings 6:20 speaks of the sanctuary "having twenty cubits in length." 
2. The word also refers to duration, the extent of a period in time. Psalms 93:5 speaks of "the duration of time": it is the length of all the days that will pass. Job 12:12 associates the length of days with wisdom: the longer one lives, the more experience one accumulates. 
3. In a more spiritual sense, the word expresses patience, perseverance, the ability to hold back and endure. Proverbs 25:15 says that "gentleness [or long-suffering] persuades the king," meaning that patience triumphs over resistance. It is a moral strength of the soul that extends over time without breaking.
H0753.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of extending, prolonging. The basic image is that of something that lasts, that occupies space in a given direction. When the word shifts from a physical sense to a moral sense, it designates this same capacity to "extend" in patience: it is the soul that prolongs, that holds firm without breaking.
H0753.emploi: The word "length" appears about 90 times in the Old Testament. It is heavily used in the description of the Tabernacle and the Temple (Exodus 25-39, 1 Kings 6-7, 2 Chronicles 3-4, Ezekiel 40-43): the length of the ark, tables, altars, walls, and doors is measured in cubits. It is a technical, very concrete word that provides the plans for these sacred constructions. But it is also found in contexts of personal duration: "the length of days" to indicate how long someone will live (Deuteronomy 30:20, Psalms 91:16, Proverbs 3:2). Finally, in Proverbs 25:15, it takes on a moral hue, that of patience that endures: "the length [of patience] of the prince changes resolutions."
H0753.portee: This word reminds us that faith is built to exact measure: it must have the right proportions, like the Temple of God. It also speaks to us of the duration of our life as a gift that God measures. And it invites us to cultivate patience and self-control, this "long-suffering" that is a powerful and discreet weapon among others. It is a virtue of one who waits, who perseveres, who does not rush.

sens: Action of extending something in time, making it last longer
Increase in duration, additional time granted
Continuation, elongation of an existence or situation
H0754.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of making something longer in duration, extending it in time. In Daniel 4:27, King Nebuchadnezzar is warned that if he renounces sin and practices righteousness, his happiness and prosperity could be prolonged — meaning they could continue longer than he would have deserved. 
2. It is also the result of this action: an increase, a delay, an additional duration granted to you. In Daniel 7:12, after the beasts (images of kingdoms) lost their dominion, a prolongation of life was given to them for a time — not eternity, but a limited period. 
3. The word carries the idea of a continuation in existence or activity, as if the time granted exceeded what was initially planned.
H0754.origine: Aramaic from the Hebrew root עֵרֶךְ (rekh), which means "valuation" or "evaluation." The Aramaic word retains the idea of a measure or estimation, here applied to duration: one measures, evaluates, prolongs time. It is an Aramaic word used in the prophetic passages of Daniel.
H0754.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament Aramaic included in Daniel, both related to God's sovereignty over life and time. In Daniel 4:27, it concerns the king's possibility of prolonging his prosperity through repentance and acts of justice. In Daniel 7:12, it describes the fate of the defeated kingdoms to which God grants temporary life. In both cases, the prolongation is a gracious act of God, limited and measured: never infinite.
H0754.portee: This word reminds us that our existence, our authority, our possessions are a gift from God for a time. It invites us to seek justice and mercy, not to guarantee immortality, but so that our lives honor God during the time He allows us. It is also a lesson in humility: earthly power is always temporary, and only God has true control over time.

sens: joint located between the thigh and the leg
physical expression of weakness or fear
gesture of submission or worship
H0755.detail:
1. The knee is the joint of the body that connects the thigh and the leg. In Daniel 5:6, King Belshazzar is seized with terror before the mysterious hand that writes on the palace wall: his knees knock together, showing how fear paralyzes the body and makes it tremble. 
2. This trembling of the knees also represents extreme weakness, the inability to stand. It is a sign of the body failing in the face of a terrifying or overwhelming reality. 
3. Bowing the knee also means to prostrate oneself, to bend before someone or something: it is the gesture of one who recognizes a superior authority or who worships.
H0755.origine: This Aramaic word derives from a root meaning "to bow" or "to bend." The Hebrew uses a word from a neighboring root to also designate the knee, the joint of the body that naturally allows one to bend and kneel. The act of bending the knees is therefore at the heart of the meaning of the word: to bend one's knees is to submit or worship.
H0755.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 5:6. It describes the moment when King Belshazzar, confronted with the supernatural writing on the wall of his impious feast, is seized with fear: his knees begin to tremble and knock together. It is a stark portrait of the physical panic of one who, faced with God, can only falter.
H0755.portee: This passage teaches that in the face of the manifestation of divine judgment, human strength collapses. The trembling of the king's knees shows that no earthly power can stand before God: it is a call to respect the holiness and majesty of the Creator.

sens: Ancient city of Mesopotamia
Inhabitants of this city, the Erechites
H0756.detail:
1. Erech was an important city of Babylon, one of the oldest Mesopotamian cities, located in what is now southern Iraq. It appears in the Bible as one of the cities whose inhabitants opposed the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile (Ezra 4:9). 

2. The term also designates the citizens or representatives of Erech — the Erechites — who, along with delegates from other Babylonian and Elamite cities, wrote a letter to the Persian king to contest the work of the Jews returning from captivity.
H0756.origine: The Aramaic name אַרְכְּוָיֵא (arkevaya) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word אֶרֶךְ (Erech), which designates this ancient Mesopotamian city. The term "Archvites" in Old French came from the idea that the name meant "lengthy" (long, durable), but it is simply the proper name of the city, transliterated from Babylonian. This city was one of the great urban centers of the ancient world.
H0756.emploi: Erech appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:9, in a specific historical context: upon returning from the Babylonian exile (around 536 B.C.), the Jews are reconstructing the temple in Jerusalem. The inhabitants of several Mesopotamian cities, including Erech, file an official complaint with King Artaxerxes to stop this work. The word appears among a list of Babylonian cities, showing the coordinated opposition of the populations of the Persian kingdom against the project of the repatriates.
H0756.portee: This passage reminds us that the restoration of God's people faced concrete obstacles, not only from immediate neighbors but also from powerful regional interests. It shows how the faith of the repatriates asserted itself in the face of institutional and administrative adversity.

sens: inhabitant ou originaire d'Arach, une ville de la montagne d'Éphraïm
H0757.detail: 1. The word designates an inhabitant of the city of Arach (or Archi), mentioned in Joshua 16:2 as a locality in the mountainous region of Ephraim, in central Israel. The demonym "Arkite" particularly applies to Hushai, the faithful friend of King David, who is found in the accounts of Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15:32 and following) and who becomes his trusted advisor.
H0757.origine: The word is a Hebrew demonym formed from the name of the city of Arach (אָרַח). The exact meaning of the city's name remains uncertain, but some scholars suggest that it means "long" or "extended," perhaps referring to the geography of the territory. The suffix -י (-i) transforms the name of the place into an adjective or demonym to designate its inhabitants.
H0757.emploi: The term appears six times in Scripture, always to qualify Hushai. It first appears in Joshua 16:2 during the description of the borders of Judah and the house of Joseph. Then, all subsequent mentions focus on the account of Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15–17) and in the list of David's officers (1 Chronicles 27:33), where Hushai the Arkite is presented as a friend of the king and a valuable advisor. His counsel prevails over that of Ahithophel, thus saving David from destruction.
H0757.portee: This word reminds us that God uses men from all backgrounds to accomplish His purposes. Hushai the Arkite, coming from a small town, becomes a key instrument to protect the Lord's anointed king in a time of crisis. His faithfulness and wisdom show that a person's worth does not depend on their social or geographical status, but on their heart towards God and their trust in Him.

sens: Fils de Sem, ancêtre des Araméens
Peuple araméen ou syrien
Région ou royaume des Araméens
H0758G.detail:
1. Aram is primarily a man: the son of Shem (himself the son of Noah), mentioned at the beginning of Genesis among the descendants of Noah who repopulated the earth after the flood (Genesis 10:22). He has four sons: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash, who found their own lineages (Genesis 10:23).
2. The name Aram then designates the people and nation that descends from this ancestor: the Arameans or Syrians. In 1 Chronicles 2:23, the "Syrians" are mentioned as conquering towns, showing that the people descended from Aram form a distinct and powerful group in the ancient Near East.
3. By extension, Aram becomes the name of the region or kingdom that this people inhabits and governs — what is called Syria in translations, a land to the north and east of Canaan.
H0758G.origine: The name literally means "exalted" in Hebrew, evoking a high or honorable position. It is a typical ancestor name in the genealogies of the Flood, establishing the descent of the peoples of the known world at the time of the Patriarchs. The same word designates both the person, his descendants, and his territory — a common usage in biblical Hebrew.
H0758G.emploi: Aram appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in genealogical lists. In Genesis 10:22 and 1 Chronicles 1:17, he is listed among the sons of Shem, establishing his place in the genealogical tree of humanity after the flood. Genesis 10:23 and 1 Chronicles 1:17 enumerate his four sons, showing how his descendants populate a territory that will become known as Arameans or Syrians. A fifth occurrence in 1 Chronicles 2:23 uses the word "Syrians" to refer to the people descended from Aram, illustrating the continuity between the ancestor and his nation.

sens: Petit-fils de Nahor, fils de Kemuel
H0758H.detail: Aram is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:21. He is the son of Kemuel, who is himself the son of Nahor (the brother of Abraham). Thus, he is a distant cousin of Abraham. His name means "exalted" in Hebrew.
H0758H.origine: The name "Aram" literally means "exalted" in Hebrew. This same name also designates, in other biblical passages, the region of Syria and the people of the Arameans; it is possible that this character is an ancestor of the Aramean people, or that the name of the people took its name from him. The Hebrew root evokes elevation and dignity.
H0758H.emploi: Aram appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 22:21, where he is named among the sons of Nahor. He is listed in the genealogy of Abraham's close ancestors, alongside his brothers Uz and Buz. This brief mention places him in the patriarchal history without any personal action reported about him.

sens: Homme de la tribu d'Asher
Personnage de l'époque de la Monarchie divisée
H0758J.detail:
1. Aram is a man from the tribe of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He belongs to the family of Shamer and is the brother of Achi, Rohega, and Hubba, as indicated in the genealogical record of 1 Chronicles 7:34.
2. This character lives during the period of the divided monarchy (when the northern and southern kingdoms had separated). He appears only once in the Bible, in this genealogical list that preserves the memory of Israelite families.
H0758J.origine: The name Aram means "exalted" in Hebrew. It shares its root with other important biblical names: the land of Aram (ancient Syria) and the people of the Arameans, whom the Bible often mentions as neighbors and sometimes enemies of Israel. This same name has been borne by other biblical figures, including a son of Shem and a grandson of Nahor, but here it designates this specific member of the tribe of Asher.
H0758J.emploi: Aram is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:34, in a genealogy of the tribe of Asher. He simply appears as one of the four sons of Shamer, alongside his brothers. These genealogical lists aimed to preserve the memory of Israelite families after the exile, showing that each tribe maintained its heritage and family lineages.

sens: people and region of the northern Levant, speaking Aramaic
inhabitants of this region, the Arameans
military allies of neighboring kingdoms of Israel
H0758K.detail: 1. Aram refers to the Aramean people and their territory, located to the north and northeast of Israel, in what is today called ancient Syria. It is a rich region well-positioned on trade routes, with several important kingdoms. 2. The Arameans are the inhabitants of Aram, a Semitic people speaking Aramaic, a language very close to Hebrew. They form several distinct states, some of which rival Israel and Judah. 3. During the time of King David, Aram is a military power: in 1 Chronicles 19:6, the sons of Ammon hire Syrian mercenaries to fight against Israel, demonstrating the military importance of Aram and its ties with Israel's enemies.
H0758K.origine: The name Aram means "the exalted" or "the elevated" in Hebrew, perhaps reflecting the high geographical position of this territory or its prestige. The Aramaic language, spoken by Aram, gradually becomes the diplomatic language of the ancient Near East and will eventually deeply influence the Middle Eastern world after the Babylonian exile.
H0758K.emploi: Aram appears regularly in the Bible to designate this people and territory with which Israel has complex relationships: sometimes allies, sometimes enemies, sometimes vassals. In 1 Chronicles 19:6, we see the Arameans of Maacah and Zobah engaged as mercenary soldiers against David. Later, Aramean kings like Ben-Hadad and Hazael become major adversaries of the northern and southern kingdoms. Aramaic also becomes the lingua franca of the Neo-Babylonian empire.
H0758K.portee: Aram reminds the reader that the history of Israel does not take place in isolation, but in a complex regional context where neighboring peoples play important roles, sometimes as allies, sometimes as enemies. It is also a reminder that God directs the history of all peoples, not just that of Israel.

sens: Region of Mesopotamia, in Upper Syria, cradle of Abraham's family
H0758L.detail: Paddan-Aram is the name of a region located in Upper Mesopotamia, in the northern part of present-day Syria. It is where Bethuel and Laban lived, the parents and brother of Rebecca, mother of Isaac and Jacob. Abraham sends his servant there to find a wife for Isaac (Genesis 25:20), and Isaac sends Jacob there to take a wife from Laban (Genesis 28:2-7). Jacob stays there for a long time, acquires flocks and goods, and then returns to Canaan (Genesis 31:18). This region is the point of origin for Jacob's immediate ancestors, which explains why it holds crucial importance in the history of Genesis: it is from there that the wives of Abraham's lineage come, ensuring a descent "from the family" and not "from the daughters of Canaan."
H0758L.origine: The Hebrew word אֲרָם (Aram) literally means "exalted" or "elevated." Aram is also the name of a son of Shem and an ancient Syrian region inhabited by the Arameans. Paddan means "field" or "way" (from the root padah), hence "Paddan-Aram": "the field of Aram" or "the plain of Aram." This geographical name precisely designates the northern Mesopotamian region where Abraham had his family origins.
H0758L.emploi: Paddan-Aram appears exclusively in the narrative of Genesis, particularly in chapters 25 to 35, which recount the story of Isaac and Jacob. The term appears only 6 times in the provided usages (Genesis 25:20; 28:2, 5, 6, 7; 31:18), always in relation to marriage and family alliances. Jacob goes there to find a wife, stays with Laban, accumulates goods and livestock, and then returns to Canaan. This region represents the earthly point of attachment of the promise made to Abraham: it is from there that the mothers of the patriarchs come, ensuring the continuity of the chosen lineage.
H0758L.portee: Paddan-Aram reminds us that Abraham's faith was not just an internal matter, but was rooted in concrete obedience: obeying God by seeking a suitable wife, far from the idolatrous influences of Canaan. For the Christian reader, this place symbolizes the importance of family faithfulness and the choice of companions according to God's will, not according to worldly conventions.

sens: Region of Northern Mesopotamia to the northeast of the promised land, inhabited by the Arameans
The Aramean or Syrian people who inhabit it
Territory of the Aramean kingdoms bordering Israel
H0758M.detail:
1. Syria is the geographical region that extends to the north and northeast of the land of Israel, in Northern Mesopotamia. It is an ancient and prosperous land, where the Aramean peoples settled. It is encountered in the accounts of conquests: David subdues Syria after his victory over Hadadezer, king of Zobah (2 Samuel 8:12).
2. The Syrians or Arameans are the people who inhabit this region. They form powerful kingdoms and maintain varied relations with Israel — sometimes enemies (as during the victory David wins over them in 2 Samuel 8:13), sometimes in commercial or diplomatic relations.
3. More broadly, the name designates the neighboring Aramean kingdoms of the promised land, such as those that threaten King Jehoshaphat and advance against Judah from across the sea towards Syria (2 Chronicles 20:2).
H0758M.origine: The Hebrew word אֲרָם (Aram) originally designates the region and the people of the Arameans, who occupied Northern Mesopotamia and spoke Aramaic, a Semitic language close to Hebrew. The name Aram appears in biblical genealogies as the ancestor of the Aramean peoples. The region was known to the Hebrews as a major contact zone: Abraham comes from Ur in Mesopotamia, Laban the Aramean lives in Upper Mesopotamia, and the Israelites are well acquainted with the Aramean peoples that border them.
H0758M.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided texts, always to designate Syria or the Syrians. In 2 Samuel 8:12-13, the context is that of David's conquests: he subdues the Syrian king Hadadezer and wins a great victory over the Syrians, showing that Aram represents a formidable military power. In 2 Chronicles 20:2, a multitude advances against Jehoshaphat from Syria, indicating that the region remains a source of threats for Judah in later periods. These usages show that Syria and the Syrians are major forces with which the kings of Israel must contend.
H0758M.portee: For the Christian reader, Syria reminds us that the people of Israel exist within a larger geopolitical world, where God controls events and victories (David victorious through God) as well as threats. These passages illustrate how God accompanies His people in regional conflicts and confirms Israel's central role in the history of the ancient Near East.

sens: Region of the Middle East between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
Territory of the Arameans, a neighboring people often in rivalry with Israel
H0758N.detail:
1. Mesopotamia is the fertile region located between two great rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, in Western Asia. It is where the great ancient civilizations (Babylon, Nineveh) were born. In the Bible, it is also called "Aram-Naharaim," which literally means "Aram of the two rivers." 
2. Mesopotamia also refers to the territory of the Arameans, a Semitic people who lived in this region and had complex relationships with Israel — sometimes allies, sometimes enemies. In Judges 3:10, Cushan-Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, oppresses Israel, showing that this region was powerful enough to threaten the young Hebrew people.
H0758N.origine: The name "Aram" likely comes from a root meaning "exalted" or "high." The Arameans were a group of Semitic peoples who settled between the two rivers and later dispersed throughout the Levant (Syria, Mesopotamia). In Greek, this territory is called "Mesopotamia," a word composed of "mesos" (middle) and "potamos" (river), which literally means "between the rivers."
H0758N.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond 1910 translation, in Judges 3:10, where it refers to the kingdom of Cushan-Rishathaim. This king comes from the North and oppresses Israel for eight years before God raises up Othniel to deliver His people. This passage shows that Mesopotamia was an external power capable of dominating Israel, which explains the strategic importance of this region in the political issues of the ancient Middle East.
H0758N.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage reminds us that even when Israel is dominated by foreign powers, God does not abandon them: He raises up a deliverer and grants victory. It is an invitation to trust in divine deliverance in the face of trials, regardless of their origin.

sens: Historical region of northwestern Mesopotamia
People of the Levant in antiquity
Homeland of the ancestors of Israel
H0758O.detail: Aram refers to the historical region that occupies northwestern Mesopotamia, between the Mediterranean and the Euphrates, roughly corresponding to modern-day Syria. It is the territory of the Arameans, an ancient people of the Levant who played an important role in the history of the ancient Near East. Aram is also the land where the ancestors of Israel have their roots: it is where Jacob fled and served to obtain a wife, Rachel (Hosea 12:13). This land is sometimes also called Paddan-Aram, literally "the plain of Aram."
H0758O.origine: The name Aram means "exalted" in Hebrew. It refers both to a geographical region and a people. The Arameans left a deep cultural and linguistic imprint on the ancient Near East, to the point that Aramaic became a major commercial and diplomatic language. This people has close genealogical ties with Israel: Aram is a son of Shem according to the biblical genealogy.
H0758O.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond as a proper noun in the strict sense (Hosea 12:13), where it refers to the land that Jacob left while fleeing from his brother Esau. This passage recalls the story of Jacob fleeing to Mesopotamia, where he served his uncle Laban to win his wives. The biblical context establishes Aram as the cradle of the ancestors of Israel, a place rich in family history and divine providence.
H0758O.portee: Aram reminds readers that the roots of Israel are humble: before being the chosen people, the ancestors of Israel were migrants, strangers in a foreign land. This memory encourages believers to recognize God's hand in trials and displacements, and to remain confident in His promise even in exile or migration.

sens: Sumptuous building where a king or great person resides
Fortified building, citadel, or fortress
Set of important constructions in a city
H0759G.detail:
1. The palace is primarily the royal residence, the magnificent building where the king lives and exercises his power. Zimri, seeing the city taken by the enemy, "withdrew into the palace of the king's house" (1 Kings 16:18), seeking refuge in this place of prestige and strength. It is the center of political and administrative power.

2. The word also refers to a fortified structure capable of withstanding attacks: a fortress or citadel. When the Lord acts in judgment against Jerusalem, He "has consumed all its palaces, He has destroyed its fortresses" (Lamentations 2:5), highlighting the defensive power of these structures. Psalms 48:14 invites to "consider its palaces," meaning to observe the imposing constructions of Jerusalem that protect it.

3. By extension, the term can refer to all the major buildings of a city, its significant edifices. When fire consumes "the palaces of Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 17:27), it refers to the important constructions that make up the city.
H0759G.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְמוֹן (armon) comes from a root that evokes the idea of height and solidity — the image of the palace as an elevated, durable, and fortified edifice. This root is related to other Hebrew words designating fortresses and heights. The term appears throughout biblical history to describe royal residences and major defensive structures, both in Israel and in Judah.
H0759G.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books, the Psalms, and the prophets. It regularly refers to the royal palace of Jerusalem or other kingdoms (1 Kings 16:18), sometimes in the singular for the king's residence itself, sometimes in the plural for all the important edifices of a city. In prophetic passages, particularly in Jeremiah and Lamentations, the palace becomes a symbol of the political and military greatness of Israel and Judah: its burning or destruction illustrates divine judgment and the collapse of national power. Isaiah 32:14 describes an abandoned palace, an image of punishment and desolation.
H0759G.portee: Understanding what the palace means in Scripture helps the reader grasp how the Bible views human power: as an imposing construction, but fragile in the face of God's judgment. The prophets use the destruction of the palace to illustrate that no earthly power, however well fortified, escapes the will of the Lord. It is a call not to place trust in the visible forces of the world, but in the one who alone remains eternal.

sens: Royal residence, the dwelling of the king and his court
Fortified building, citadel or fortress
Imposing building or prestigious construction
Symbol of political power and wealth
H0759H.detail:
1. The palace is the grand residence of the king, the place where he reigns and where his family and servants live. It is the heart of political power. In prophecies of threat, the palaces of enemy cities are the buildings that God destroys to punish unfaithfulness: "I will send fire upon the walls of Tyre, and it shall devour its palaces" (Amos 1:10).
2. The palace is also a fortress, a defensive structure meant to protect the city and those who govern it. In Amos 3:9, the prophet denounces that the palaces of Israel are filled with violence, showing that these strongholds should have been symbols of justice and protection.
3. By extension, the word designates any building of great importance or beauty: in Isaiah 34:13, when desolation comes, the palaces become dens for wild beasts, underscoring their total downfall. Proverbs 18:19 uses the word figuratively to speak of a fortified soul.
4. The palace represents human power in all its height and apparent solidity. But the Bible often shows it vulnerable to God's justice: thorns shall grow in its palaces (Isaiah 34:13), and fire shall consume them (Hosea 8:14).
H0759H.origine: The Hebrew word אַרְמוֹן (armon) comes from a root that evokes strength and solidity. Its basic image is that of an elevated, protected, imposing structure — the dwelling of power. It is found in other ancient Near Eastern languages with a similar meaning. The underlying root suggests something raised, erected: a building that rises above the ordinary city, visible from afar.
H0759H.emploi: The word appears eighteen times in the Bible, mostly in the judgment prophets (Amos, Jeremiah, Hosea) and the Psalms. In the oracles against the nations (Amos 1-2), the refrain "I will send fire upon the walls... and it shall devour the palaces" shows that the palace is the preferred target of divine wrath: it is where human power boasts, and it is there that it is broken. In the prophets, the palace is never neutral: it symbolizes either the greatness of the faithful king (Psalms 122:7, where peace is wished in the palaces of Zion), or the corruption of unfaithful princes (Amos 3:10, where the palaces are filled with plunder). In Isaiah 25:2, God destroys the fortified city, its palaces are brought to nothing. The word can also refer to the concrete and architectural sense (Proverbs 18:19).
H0759H.portee: This word reminds the believer that the material and architectural power of empires — however impressive — remains fragile in the face of God's justice and sovereignty. The palace, a symbol of human power, can become ruin: this image calls not to rely on the forces of this world, but on God alone. For Israel, the palace of Jerusalem (David's dwelling) represents the hope of God's reign on earth; its temporary destruction by exile is also a promise of future restoration.

sens: Aramean region located northeast of Damascus
Territory of an enemy power of King David
Vassal state in ancient Near Eastern conflicts
H0760.detail:
1. Tsoba is an Aramean region, meaning inhabited by the Arameans, a people established northeast of Damascus (the current capital of Syria). It represents a center of political and military power in this area of the ancient Levant.
2. The Bible mentions Tsoba as an enemy that King David fought against. In Psalms 60:2, it is written that David waged war "against the Syrians of Tsoba" — these were significant military conflicts of his time.
3. Tsoba was an Aramean state or principality that exerted regional influence. These small Aramean kingdoms formed a mosaic of rival powers in the Syrian area of antiquity.
H0760.origine: The name Tsoba likely means "high place" or "citadel," evoking a fortified location or a place of command at a height — an image suggested by its elevated location northeast of Damascus. It is an Aramean name, specific to the territories and Aramean peoples of the biblical Near East.
H0760.emploi: Tsoba appears only once in the Segond translations, in Psalms 60:2. The context indicates that King David led a military expedition against this Aramean territory; after a victory over the Syrians of Tsoba, Joab returned and achieved an additional victory by defeating the Edomites in the valley of salt. Thus, Tsoba represents a major adversary of King David during his campaigns to consolidate power in the ancient Near East.
H0760.portee: This geographical proper noun reminds the reader that King David's power extended through victorious military campaigns against neighboring peoples — which corresponded to the political project of establishing a powerful kingdom in the region. It is a concrete historical detail that anchors faith in the real history of nations.

sens: Woman from Syria or Aram
H0761G.detail: The only biblical use of this word refers to a Syrian or Aramean woman, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:14 as the wife of Manasseh and mother of Makir. She represents a union between Manasseh and a woman from the Aramean people, illustrating marital alliances between Israel and neighboring peoples.
H0761G.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew noun "Aram," which designates the country and people of Syria. The addition of the feminine suffix in Hebrew transforms "Aramite" (related to Aram) into "Aramean" (woman from Aram). The root "Aram" likely means "high" or "exalted," which may reflect the geographical significance of this region north of Israel.
H0761G.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:14, in the genealogical context of the tribe of Manasseh. It specifically designates the foreign wife that Manasseh took, highlighting the non-Israelite origin of this woman and her descendants.
H0761G.portee: This passage reminds us that the Israelites had contacts and alliances with neighboring peoples, including the Arameans. It also shows that Israel's identity was not absolutely closed, even though the Law warned against unions that would lead them away from their God.

sens: Inhabitant or native of Syria (Aram)
Warrior or soldier from Syria
Person or people foreign to the kingdoms of Israel and Judah
H0761H.detail:
1. The word designates a person from Syria (Aram in Hebrew), the region north of Israel. In 2 Kings 5:20, Gehazi refers to Naaman as a "Syrian," meaning a foreigner from this distant land who came to be healed of his leprosy.
2. Often, the text uses this word to refer to Syrian warriors or soldiers in conflict with the Israelite kingdoms. In 2 Kings 8:28-29 and 9:15, the "Syrians" are those who wounded King Joram in battle, under the command of Hazael, king of Syria.
3. More broadly, "Syrian" designates anything foreign to the world of Israel and Judah — a geographical and political otherness that underscores the separation between peoples.
H0761H.origine: The word comes from the root "Aram" (אֲרָם), which designates the region of Syria. The name "Aram" itself would mean "exalted" or "high land." The Arameans, inhabitants of Aram, gradually became a major people in the ancient Near East, known for their trade and language. The Hebrew word "Syrian" (אֲרַמִּי) is formed by adding the suffix of belonging to the name of the country, as if to say "one from Aram."
H0761H.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always in 2 Kings (5:20; 8:28, 29; 9:15). These four uses all concern military relations between the kingdoms of Israel and Judah with Syria, particularly conflicts with Hazael, king of Syria. In 2 Kings 5:20, it refers to Naaman, an individual foreign character. In the other three verses (8:28, 29; 9:15), the plural word "Syrians" refers to the Syrian military troops confronting Joram. The usage remains factual and contextual, without particular moral connotation.
H0761H.portee: This word reminds us that biblical history unfolds in a concrete world of distinct peoples, with their languages, territories, and conflicts. Naaman the Syrian, despite his foreign origin, becomes the object of divine mercy and miraculous healing — a lesson about God's love that transcends national boundaries.

sens: Inhabitant or originating from Aram, an ancient Near Eastern region
Person speaking Aramaic or of Aramean culture
Ethnic group neighboring Israel
H0761J.detail: 1. An Aramean is a person from Aram, an ancient Near Eastern region located between Mesopotamia and the Levant. Bethuel and Laban, who play major roles in the stories of Abraham and Jacob, are referred to as Arameans (Genesis 25:20; 28:5). 2. The term also denotes belonging to a specific culture and language: the Arameans spoke Aramaic and had their own customs. Laban, the Aramean, represents this people in the biblical narrative (Genesis 31:20, 24). 3. In Deuteronomy 26:5, the word also evokes nomadism: the Israelite confesses that "my father was a wandering Aramean," highlighting Israel's wandering Near Eastern origins before settling in Egypt and then Canaan.
H0761J.origine: The Hebrew word אֲרַמִּי comes from the name of the region of Aram (אָרָם), whose etymology means "exalted." Aram designates the territory controlled by this people, located between Mesopotamia and the Levant. The Aramaic form of the word also exists in Aramaic itself, reflecting the mutual influence between Hebrew and Aramaic in ancient Near Eastern life.
H0761J.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to qualify characters related to Paddan-Aram or the region of Aram. Bethuel and Laban are called "the Aramean" several times (Genesis 25:20; 28:5; 31:20, 24), indicating their identity and distinct origin from Israel. The usage culminates in the confession of faith in Deuteronomy 26:5, where an Israelite acknowledges that his ancestor was a "wandering Aramean" — that is, the patriarchs themselves came from this people before God separated them. The term thus serves to remind of Israel's geographical and ethnic roots.
H0761J.portee: This word makes visible the continuity of divine providence: God called Abraham, a man from Aram, to make him the father of a great nation. By remembering that he comes from an Aramean, the Israelite acknowledges God's free election and faithfulness to a people whose origins were ordinary and distant. This calls for humility and gratitude.

sens: the language spoken and written in Aram and in the ancient Near East
the idiom of the kingdom of Aram and neighboring peoples
the dialect used in diplomatic and administrative exchanges
H0762.detail:
1. Aramaic is the language of the people of Aram, a region of the ancient Near East. It is a Semitic language, a cousin of Hebrew, which gradually became established as the international language of trade and politics. In 2 Kings 18:26, the Judean officials ask an Assyrian ambassador to speak in Aramaic rather than Hebrew, as it is the diplomatic language that all scribes understand.
2. Aramaic became the language of Persian administration: in Ezra 4:7, an official letter addressed to King Artaxerxes is transcribed in Aramaic characters and translated into Aramaic, showing that it is the language of royal bureaucracy. This is why portions of the later Old Testament (Daniel and Ezra) are written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.
3. When Daniel 2:4 notes that "the Chaldeans answered the king in Aramaic," it confirms that Aramaic had become the common lingua franca, even for Chaldean scholars and priests, as was the case for many peoples of the Near East.
H0762.origine: The word Aramaic comes from the root of the name Aram, the country in northwestern Mesopotamia. Aramaic is a historical Semitic language that later gave rise to several dialects (Syriac, Mandaic, Neo-Aramaic). The language bears the name of its people of origin, as is customary for ancient idioms.
H0762.emploi: The word Aramaic appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate this specific language. It is mainly found in narratives concerning diplomatic contacts with foreign powers: the Judean officials under Hezekiah ask Rabshekah, the Assyrian envoy, for it (2 Kings 18:26 and Isaiah 36:11, two parallel passages). In the Persian period, Aramaic is the official language of the royal chancery (Ezra 4:7). The Book of Daniel uses the term regarding the Chaldeans' response to King Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:4), and indeed the Book of Daniel itself shifts to Aramaic narrative shortly after this verse. This shows that Aramaic is recognized as the language of international prestige, especially from the Babylonian exile onward.
H0762.portee: For the contemporary Christian, this word reminds us how God allowed the Judeans to maintain their religious and linguistic identity (Hebrew) while adapting to political realities that required knowledge of other languages and cultures. It is also a sign of the high historical significance of the Bible: it does not merely report stories; it integrates linguistic and administrative details that reflect the complexity of the ancient world. Finally, the Aramaic in the Book of Daniel is a reminder that God inspired his prophets even when they wrote in the languages of their rulers.

sens: Region between the Euphrates and Tigris, cradle of great ancient civilizations
Territory of the Aramean kingdoms in the northwest
Area of origin for the ancestors of Israel and place of foreign power
H0763G.detail:
1. Mesopotamia is the fertile region located between the two great rivers of the Near East, the Euphrates and the Tigris. The name literally means "Aram of the two rivers" in Hebrew: it is a historically significant land, the cradle of major civilizations and a crossroads of trade routes. It is mentioned when Abraham sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac (Genesis 24:10).
2. In the biblical context, Mesopotamia mainly refers to the Aramean kingdoms of the northwest, where the Aramaic-speaking peoples lived. It is from there that Balaam, the diviner hired to curse Israel, came, and it is there that the Syrians of Mesopotamia hired chariots and horsemen (Deuteronomy 23:4 and 1 Chronicles 19:6).
3. For Israel, Mesopotamia represents both the cradle of its origins — Abraham came from there — and a source of threat: Cushan-Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, oppressed Israel for eight years during the time of the Judges (Judges 3:8).
H0763G.origine: The Hebrew name אֲרַם נַהֲרַיִם (Aram naharaïm) literally means "Aram of the two rivers." Aram designates the Aramean peoples and their lands; nahara means river, and naharaïm (two rivers) refers to the Euphrates and Tigris that surround this fertile region. Geographically, the Greek term Mesopotamia ("between two rivers") conveys exactly this same idea.
H0763G.emploi: The name Mesopotamia appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate this historical region of the Near East. It is first the starting point of Abraham's servant's journey (Genesis 24:10), recalling the roots of Israel's ancestors. It is then associated with foreign powers: Balaam the diviner comes from Mesopotamia to curse Israel (Deuteronomy 23:4), Cushan-Rishathaim, a king of Mesopotamia, oppressed the Israelites (Judges 3:8), and the Syrian kingdoms of Mesopotamia provided mercenaries and chariots to those who fought David (1 Chronicles 19:6). The region thus embodies both the distant origins of the people and a potential threat.
H0763G.portee: For the Christian reader, Mesopotamia reminds us that the ancestors of the faith came from a distant and idolatrous land, and that God called them out — Abraham leaves Ur of the Chaldeans to follow God (see Genesis 11:31). It also evokes how the Lord protects his people against the powers of the world that seek to destroy them: threats from Mesopotamia are defeated or halted by God.

sens: The region located between the two major rivers of the Middle East, the Tigris and the Euphrates
The territory called Aram-Naharaim by the Arameans, corresponding to northeastern Syria
Historical region from which the Syrian or Aramean peoples mentioned in Psalms 60 originated
H0763H.detail:
1. The Hebrew name "Aram Naharaim" literally means "Aram of the two rivers": the fertile and densely populated region that extends between the Tigris and the Euphrates in Upper Mesopotamia. This area was the cradle of ancient civilizations and an important crossroads of the ancient world.
2. In Psalms 60:2, this term refers to the Syrian or Aramean peoples who inhabited this region and who waged war against Israel. It is the territory from which the enemies that David fought originated, showing that this region was a distinct political and military power separate from the rest of Syria.
H0763H.origine: The word is composed of two Aramaic elements: "Aram" means Syria or the Aramean people, and "Naharaim" comes from the root "nahar" (river), in the dual "naharaim" (the two rivers). This name geographically describes the region by its major characteristic: its positioning between two great waterways. The Greeks called this region "Mesopotamia" ("between the rivers"), accurately translating this same notion.
H0763H.emploi: This term appears only once in the Bible in Psalms 60:2, in the context of David's wars. It specifically designates the Syrian or Aramean adversaries that the king of Israel fought, alongside the Syrians of Zobah. This passage shows that Mesopotamia was a territory recognized as a distinct military power during the time of the Psalm, attesting to the political and strategic importance of this region for Israel.
H0763H.portee: This name reminds us that biblical geography encompasses regions and peoples beyond the borders of Israel, and that Israel's conflicts were situated within a broader geopolitical context of the ancient Middle East. It also shows how the two great rivers of the Middle East (Tigris and Euphrates) marked the limits of the known world for the ancient Hebrews.

sens: Son of Saul and Rizpah, of the tribe of Benjamin
H0764.detail: Armoni is a character from the Old Testament, son of King Saul and Rizpah. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 21:8, during a tragic episode where King David delivers him, along with his brother Mephibosheth, to the Gibeonites for execution, in order to atone for an ancient violation of the treaty that Saul had committed against this nation.
H0764.origine: The name Armoni literally means "one of the palace" or "man of the palace," reflecting his status as a royal son. It comes from the Hebrew root חצר (hétser), which designates the court or royal palace. It is a name that emphasizes belonging to the royal house of Saul, the first king of Israel.
H0764.emploi: Armoni appears only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Samuel 21:8. He is mentioned alongside his half-brother Mephibosheth, as one of the two sons that Rizpah bore to Saul. This single verse places him in a context of restorative justice: David, to appease divine wrath provoked by Saul's crimes against the Gibeonites, hands them over to this nation for execution. Although the text provides no details about his personal life, it shows him as a victim of the consequences of his father's sins.
H0764.portee: The mention of Armoni reminds us that the actions of leaders can have tragic consequences for their descendants and for innocents. His story encourages the reader to reflect on the responsibility of power and how sin spreads, but also on the cost of restorative justice and reconciliation between peoples.

sens: Son of Dishan and descendant of Esau
H0765.detail: Aran is a man from the patriarchal era, son of Dishan. He belongs to the lineage of Esau, the ancestor of the Edomites. He is encountered only in the genealogical lists of Genesis and 1 Chronicles, where he is presented alongside his brother Uz as one of the descendants of Esau.
H0765.origine: The name Aran means "joyful" in Hebrew. It designates a minor character in the patriarchal narrative, known only by these two genealogical mentions that establish his place in the descent of Esau and the Edomite people.
H0765.emploi: Aran appears only twice in the Bible, in Genesis 36:28 and in 1 Chronicles 1:42, in passages that enumerate the descendants of Esau. These two verses are actually the same genealogical content, one copied from the other: both cite him as the son of Dishan and brother of Uz. He is a minor figure in the Edomite genealogy, without any event or word that characterizes him.

sens: Evergreen coniferous tree
Wood from this tree, used in construction and carpentry
H0766.detail:
1. The pine is a large forest tree with persistent needles and hard, resinous wood. It grows quickly, making it valuable for construction and carpentry work. In Isaiah 44:14, the prophet speaks of one who "plants pines" to see them grow thanks to the rain, illustrating how man cultivates the resources of nature.
2. By extension, the word also refers to pine wood itself, a sought-after material for its strength and durability. This wood was used to make frameworks, ship masts, and other important structural elements.
H0766.origine: The Hebrew word אֹרֶן (oren) specifically designates the pine, a characteristic tree of the ancient Middle East. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of strength or firmness, a quality related to the solidity of pine wood. This word is distinguished from other forest trees mentioned in the same passage (cedars, oaks), each having its particular properties.
H0766.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 44:14), in a context of prophetic critique against idolatry. The prophet Isaiah ironically describes how an idolater cuts wood from various species — cedars, oaks — and chooses some to carve into a god. The pine is mentioned among the ordinary trees of the forest, highlighting the contrast between a simple natural material and the object of worship that is made from it.
H0766.portee: This passage invites the believer to recognize that idols are merely ordinary wood, shaped by human hands. The pine, a common tree that the rain helps to grow, symbolizes the vanity of transforming a material creation into an object of veneration. It is a call to place one's faith in God alone, not in objects made by man.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the united monarchy
H0767.detail: Oren is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, living at the time when the twelve tribes formed a united kingdom. He is the son of Jerachmeel and the brother of Ram, Buna, Otsem, Ahijah, and Onam. His only biblical mention is found in 1 Chronicles 2:25, where he is listed in the genealogy of the clan of Judah.
H0767.origine: The name Oren means "cedar" in Hebrew, the noble and durable tree of the Bible. This name evokes solidity and strength, qualities often associated with this precious wood. Oren is part of a long Davidic genealogy that establishes the roots of the chosen people.
H0767.emploi: Oren appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:25. This mention is found in the genealogy of the sons of Jerachmeel, the firstborn of Hezron, who himself descended from Judah. These genealogical lists in Chronicles preserve the memory of the clans and families that constituted the tribe of Judah before and during the united monarchy. The context of this genealogy is that of establishing the tribal and familial structures of the people of Israel.

sens: small animal resembling a rabbit, with long ears and strong hind legs
animal declared unclean in the Mosaic law, forbidden for consumption
H0768.detail:
1. The hare is a small wild animal, probably close to the rabbit in appearance, with particularly developed hind legs that allow it to run fast. It is a herbivorous rodent. In Leviticus 11:6, it is mentioned as an animal that "chews the cud," meaning it seems to chew like ruminants, but the expression remains enigmatic as real hares do not actually ruminate — this suggests either an ancient confusion or another animal that is now extinct or misidentified.
2. In the law of Moses, the hare is listed among the unclean animals that are forbidden for consumption by the people of Israel (Leviticus 11:6 and Deuteronomy 14:7). This prohibition is part of the dietary laws that distinguished Israel from other peoples and marked their belonging to the covenant people.
H0768.origine: The Hebrew word "arnèbeth" refers to a small wild animal with long ears. Its exact origin remains uncertain, but it belongs to the vocabulary of domestic and wild animals in the Old Testament. The word appears exclusively in the dietary lists of the Law, underscoring its importance in Israel's ritual and health concerns.
H0768.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the legislative texts of Moses: in Leviticus 11:6 and Deuteronomy 14:7. Both occurrences are in the same context — the laws of dietary purity — and repeat the same singular detail: the animal "chews the cud, but does not have split hooves." This repetition in two important legislative books shows that this classification was central to Israel's religious identity. The absence of other biblical uses suggests that the term, well established in the language, had a fixed and well-defined place in the ritual classification system.
H0768.portee: The hare reminds us that the Mosaic Law, given by God, encompassed the concrete details of daily life, including what believers eat. For the Christian, this example shows how God desired His people to stand out through obedience even in simple actions. Although Acts and the Epistle to the Romans free Christians from these dietary prohibitions, this passage invites us to reflect on practical holiness and voluntary obedience to God.

sens: Watercourse of the Palestinian Levant
Valley formed by this stream
Natural boundary between peoples
H0769.detail:
1. The Arnon is a stream (brook or river depending on the seasons) that flows in the southern desert of Palestine toward the Jordan. In Numbers 21:13, it is written that Israel "camped on the other side of the Arnon, which flows in the desert coming out of the territory of the Amorites." It is a real waterway, important for crossing the land.
2. The word also designates the valley that this watercourse carves and delineates. Deuteronomy 3:12 speaks of the "torrent of the Arnon" as a geographical landmark where the territory given to the tribes of Reuben and Gad begins, marking a space of land on either side of the riverbed.
3. The Arnon serves as a natural and political boundary: it separates Moab from the Amorites, and later the land of Israel from that of Moab. In Judges 11:13 and following, we find this role of recognized limit between nations, which each respects or disputes.
H0769.origine: The name Arnon literally means "torrent that flows with force" or "rapid watercourse" — it evokes the impetuous movement of water. It is a historically attested watercourse that still forms the boundary between present-day Jordan and the historical territories of Moab. The Hebrew word does not derive from a common biblical root: it is an ancient geographical name, rooted in the real landscape of the Levant.
H0769.emploi: The Arnon appears 23 times in the Bible, mainly in the account of the conquest (Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua) and in the poems and prayers that recall it (Judges, Isaiah, Jeremiah). As Israel advances toward Canaan, Moses commands Israel to cross the Arnon and fight Sihon, king of the Amorites (Deuteronomy 2:24). After the victory, the torrent becomes the southern boundary of the territory conquered beyond the Jordan, assigned to Reuben and Gad (Deuteronomy 3:12; Joshua 13:16). Later, Jephthah mentions it as an ancestral boundary in dispute with Ammon (Judges 11). The prophet Isaiah (16:2) and Jeremiah (48:20) will refer to it in their oracles against Moab. It is less a word whose meaning changes than a fixed and unavoidable landmark of sacred geography.

sens: Son of Hananiah, descendant of David, of the tribe of Judah
H0770.detail: Arnan is a minor character in the royal genealogy of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Hananiah and the brother of Pelatiah, Isaiah, Rephaiah, Obadiah, and Shecaniah (1 Chronicles 3:21). He belongs to the lineage of David and lived during the time of the division of the Israelite monarchy, between the reign of Solomon and the Babylonian captivity. His name appears in this genealogical list which shows how the descendants of King David continued despite the political and religious turmoil of that period.
H0770.origine: The name Arnan literally means "lion of perpetuity" or "one who shouts for joy," according to ancient etymologies. It comes from the Hebrew context where personal names often carry symbolic or prophetic significance, expressing a wish or quality that parents hoped to bestow upon their child.
H0770.emploi: Arnan appears only once in the Holy Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 3:21, in the context of a genealogy that lists the descendants of David after the Babylonian exile. This passage lists the children of Hananiah, of whom Arnan is a part. The mention of Arnan in this genealogy emphasizes that the lineage of David survived the political upheavals and was maintained, even though these descendants did not become kings: they simply represent the heirs of the promise made to David by God.

sens: A Jebusite who owned a threshing floor in Jerusalem
The owner of the land where David built the altar of the Lord
H0771.detail:
1. Ornan is a man of the Jebusite people living at the time of the united monarchy. He owns a threshing floor (a flat area) where wheat is threshed, meaning where grain is separated from chaff. When the angel of the Lord appears over Jerusalem to end the plague that strikes the people, he stands right by this threshing floor (1 Chronicles 21:15).
2. Ornan becomes a key figure in the narrative because David, at the command of the prophet Gad, must raise an altar to the Lord on this land (1 Chronicles 21:18). Ornan recognizes David, bows down, and generously offers his threshing floor and even the necessary materials: the oxen, the wood from the carts, and the wheat (1 Chronicles 21:23). It is on this threshing floor that Solomon's Temple is later built (2 Chronicles 3:1).
H0771.origine: The name "Ornan" probably means "the light has been perpetuated" in ancient Hebrew. It is a Canaanite name, which suits this Jebusite, original inhabitant of Jerusalem. The same character is also called "Araunah" in the parallel account of 2 Samuel 24, where his name bears a slightly different form. These two names refer to the same person.
H0771.emploi: Ornan appears ten times in the Scriptures, exclusively in the book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 21 and 2 Chronicles 3). He is a minor but memorable character in the account of the plague that strikes Israel during David's reign. The text first shows him threshing wheat, peacefully unaware of the drama approaching (1 Chronicles 21:20). He then appears five times in the dialogue between David and him, where he reveals his generosity, his reverence for the king, and especially his obedience to what God desires to accomplish. He accepts to give his property to David without hesitation, and even offers him the resources to build the altar. This humble yet decisive role connects him to the history of the Temple.
H0771.portee: The character of Ornan teaches the reader about God's providence: God directs events so that the land intended for the Temple is acquired at the right moment, in the king's repentance and the people's obedience. Ornan's generosity, who relinquishes his property for the service of God, also illustrates the disposition of heart that God approves. It is a reminder that God delights in using the goodwill of simple individuals to accomplish His purposes.

sens: The soil, the mineral matter where plants grow
The physical world, the entirety of created material things
The order of earthly realities, in contrast to the divine or celestial
H0772G.detail:
1. The earth primarily refers to the soil, the mineral surface where trees take root and grass grows: this is the most concrete meaning. In Daniel 4:15 and 4:23, the tree trunk must remain "in the earth" with its roots to continue living; the earth nourishes what grows in it.
2. The word extends to the entire earth, the physical world where creatures live: in Daniel 7:4, the beast "is taken from the earth," meaning lifted from the material world where it stood, and made to stand like a man. This is the earth where visible events unfold.
3. The earth can also refer to the order of changing earthly realities, in contrast to celestial and eternal realities. When something is "taken from the earth," it is like a promotion, a transition from the temporal world to another condition.
H0772G.origine: The Aramaic word אֲרַע (ara) is the direct equivalent of the Hebrew אֶרֶץ (eretz), both referring to soil and earth. This family of words is present throughout ancient Semitic languages. The Hebrew eretz primarily means the ground that is trodden and cultivated, then extends to the entire earth, the land, the world. The closely related Aramaic takes this same root and range of meanings.
H0772G.emploi: The Aramaic word אֲרַע appears three times in the Aramaic New Testament of the writers of Daniel (chapters 4 and 7). It is used in the context of Nebuchadnezzar's dream: the tree must keep its trunk "in the earth" (4:15, 4:23), rooted in the ground, alive. Then in 7:4, the beast of the dream is "taken from the earth" and made to stand on its feet. In all cases, the word refers to the physical, material ground, the concrete world from which things draw their sustenance and where they move.
H0772G.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that the Creator God has established a real physical world, where life takes root and flourishes. The trunk that remains in the earth evokes that even in humiliation and limitation, life continues if it remains anchored. The transition from the physical world to another condition (the beast taken from the earth) invites reflection on the different orders of reality that God governs.

sens: Of lower rank, value, or power
Coming after in the order of succession or greatness
H0772H.detail:
1. The word denotes what is inferior in importance, value, or power. In Daniel 2:39, the second kingdom that will arise after Babylon is said to be "lesser" than that of Nebuchadnezzar: it will be less powerful, less prestigious, even though it will still dominate over vast territories.
2. It can also qualify what comes second in a succession, in contrast to the first: the second empire is lesser than the first, thus marking a certain decline or reduction in greatness from one era to another.
H0772H.origine: This Aramaic word derives from the same root as the Hebrew eretz (אֶרֶץ), which primarily means "earth" or "soil." The meaning "lesser" or "inferior" is a specific sense of this word in Aramaic, less common than the primary meaning, but attested in the context of comparison between kingdoms.
