H0772H.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 2:39, in the interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar by the prophet Daniel. It describes the second empire of the prophetic vision as inferior to the first (the Babylonian empire). This passage is part of the dream of the four kingdoms, where each empire is compared to the previous ones according to its greatness and power.
H0772H.portee: This word reminds us of a biblical truth: earthly power is never stable and inevitably declines. The Christian learns that the kingdoms of the world, however powerful they may seem, will not last and will give way to others, even lesser. This invites us not to place our trust in human political forces, but in God alone who reigns eternally.

sens: The entirety of soil and land masses, in contrast to the sky
The entirety of the inhabitants of the world
The domain, the territory subject to authority
The world considered in its expanse and vastness
H0772I.detail:
1. The earth is primarily the soil, the material element on which one walks and that extends beneath our feet, in contrast to the sky above. In Ezra 5:11, it speaks of "servants of the God of heaven and earth," acknowledging that God reigns over these two distinct domains.
2. The word also refers to all the peoples and nations that live on it. In Daniel 4:1, King Nebuchadnezzar writes "to all peoples, nations, and men of every language, who dwell on all the earth," meaning: to all the inhabitants of the world.
3. The earth can represent the domain of a political or divine power, which extends under its authority. When it is written that the king's dominion "extends to the ends of the earth" (Daniel 4:22), it means his empire covers the known world.
4. The word finally evokes the immensity, the vastness of the entire world, particularly in the cosmic visions of Daniel where stones and kingdoms fill "the whole earth" (Daniel 2:35).
H0772I.origine: The Aramaic word אֲרַע (a.ra) is the exact equivalent of the Hebrew word אֶרֶץ (e.rets, H0776), which literally means the soil, the earth as a physical reality. These two words, Hebrew and Aramaic, share the same root and the same image: that of the firm surface on which one stands, in relation to the heavens that rise above. The transition from Hebrew to Aramaic simply reflects the linguistic context: the books of Ezra and Daniel were partially written in Aramaic, the administrative language of the Persian empire.
H0772I.emploi: The Aramaic word for "earth" appears 14 times in the Bible, exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel. These two books, composed partly in Aramaic, use it mainly in contexts of cosmic vision or royal announcements. In Ezra 5:11, it refers to God's creation in parallel with heaven. In chapters 2 and 4 of Daniel, during the great symbolic visions of King Nebuchadnezzar, the earth becomes the stage where succeeding powers unfold: it is the theater where powers are displayed. In Daniel 4:22 and 6:25, the word expresses the extent of royal power, which covers the entire world. Especially in Daniel, "the earth" embodies the world order subject to political regimes and divine sovereignty.
H0772I.portee: For the reader, the word "earth" reminds us that the visible world does not exist outside of divine order. When Daniel proclaims that God reigns over "the earth" as over the heavens, he affirms that no human empire, however powerful it may be, can escape God's control. The word invites the believer not to be impressed by earthly greatness, for they remain under divine judgment.

sens: The lowest point of a pit or hollow
The lower part of a container or hollow space
H0773.detail:
1. The word denotes the lowest point of a pit or hollow. In the account of Daniel thrown to the lions, it evokes the depth of the pit where the prophet's enemies are thrown: before they even reach the bottom, the lions seize them (Daniel 6:24). It is the image of a chasm, a deep hollow.
2. More broadly, the "bottom" is the lower part of a hollow space or container — what remains when one descends to the end. The word emphasizes the depth and the distance between the surface and the ground.
H0773.origine: This Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Jews during the Persian period) comes from the same root as the Hebrew "eretz" (אֶרֶץ), which means earth, soil, or land. The Aramaic word "ar'i" retains the concrete meaning: the earth at the bottom of things, the lowest point.
H0773.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 6:24. It describes the lion's den into which the king of Persia has the accusers of Daniel thrown. The usage highlights the depth of the pit and the impossibility of escaping the fall: the lions catch them before they even touch the bottom. It is a dramatic detail that emphasizes the swiftness and inevitability of punishment.
H0773.portee: This word reminds us that divine justice catches the guilty without delay. In the story of Daniel, those who conspired against an innocent person do not descend long before encountering their punishment — a biblical image of certain retribution.

sens: Ancient city of northern Syria
Example of a city conquered by Assyria
H0774.detail: 1. Arpad is an ancient city located in northern Syria, mentioned several times in the Bible around the 8th century BC. It often appears alongside other Syrian cities like Hamath and Damascus, indicating its regional importance (Isaiah 10:9). 2. The Bible mentions Arpad as a striking example of Assyrian military power: the prophets invoke it to show that even powerful cities and their gods could not withstand Assyrian conquest (2 Kings 18:34 and Isaiah 36:19). 3. In Jeremiah 49:23, Arpad is described as trembling and confused at the announcement of bad news, an image of a city disoriented in the face of impending disasters.
H0774.origine: The name means in Hebrew "I will be extended" or "I will be supported," possibly evoking the expansion or solidity of a fortress. Arpad is a historically well-attested city in Assyrian documents, identified with the modern site of Tell Rifaat in northern Syria.
H0774.emploi: Arpad appears 6 times in the Bible, only in the prophetic and historical books of the 8th century BC. It is mentioned in 2 Kings 18:34 and 19:13 in the context of the siege of Jerusalem by the Assyrian king Sennacherib, who boasts that his gods did not save Arpad. The three parallel passages in Isaiah (10:9, 36:19, 37:13) follow the same pattern: Arpad symbolizes the helplessness of human kingdoms against Assyrian power. In Jeremiah 49:23, it is listed among the cities judged for their sins.
H0774.portee: Arpad reminds the reader that powerful empires and human defenses, no matter how impressive, cannot stand against God's plan. The prophets use it to urge Judah to place its trust in the Lord rather than in political or military alliances. It is a lesson in humility in the face of God's judgment on the nations.

sens: Son of Shem and ancestor of the Abrahamic lineage
H0775.detail: Arpacschad is the third son of Shem (the son of Noah), mentioned in the genealogy of Genesis 10:22. He is the father of Shelah and an essential link in the genealogical chain connecting Noah to Abraham. After the flood, Shem fathered Arpacschad two years later (Genesis 11:10), and he lived 438 years, a century and a half less than his father. Arpacschad appears in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles to confirm his place in Shem's lineage, and the Gospel of Luke mentions him in the genealogy of Jesus.
H0775.origine: The name Arpacschad carries an ancient meaning, sometimes translated as "I will be broken like the breast" or an image related to nursing, though the exact meaning is not entirely clear to modern readers. What matters here is that this name belongs to the patriarchal genealogy: it marks a real character from the late antediluvian world, inserted into the canonical genealogies of the Hebrew Bible and the Greek New Testament.
H0775.emploi: Arpacschad appears nine times in the sacred texts, mainly in genealogies. He first appears in Genesis 10, the chapter of nations, where he is named among the sons of Shem (10:22) and where he fathers Shelah (10:24). Genesis 11 repeats this information with chronological details: Shem fathered him two years after the flood, at 100 years old (11:10); Arpacschad was 35 years old when he fathered Shelah (11:12); he lived 403 years after Shelah's birth (11:13). He is found in 1 Chronicles 1 to validate this genealogy. Luke 3:36 includes him in the lineage leading to Jesus, thus connecting him to the divine promise.
H0775.portee: Arpacschad reminds us that God preserved a human lineage through Noah and his sons after the judgment of the flood. He embodies the continuity of the divine promise through the ages: it is through his line that Shelah, Eber, Peleg, and ultimately Abraham pass. Recognizing Arpacschad is to acknowledge that the story of salvation has never been interrupted but has been faithfully pursued according to God's plan, despite sin and judgment.

sens: The physical expanse of soil, the planet as a solid mass
Delimited territory, region or country
The inhabited earth, with its populations
Earthly existence, as opposed to heaven or the world to come
H0776G.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the physical substance: the mass of dry land that God created ("In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth," Genesis 1:1). It is the ground on which one walks, as opposed to water and heaven. 2. A more precise sense: a delimited geographical region, a country. When the Lord says to Moses, "Go up to the land that I swore to give to Abraham," it refers to the land of Canaan, a defined area (Exodus 33:1). 3. The word can also refer to the inhabitants of a region: "all the inhabitants of the land tremble before you" (Joshua 2:9). The image shifts from the territory to those who occupy it. 4. More broadly, "earth" signifies the known world, the sphere of human existence, hence the expression "kings of the earth" (2 Chronicles 9:22): those who reign over the earthly and temporal domain.
H0776G.origine: This ancient word in Hebrew is likely related to the idea of what is solid, stable, in contrast to liquid and void. It shares a common root with words meaning "to be firm" or "to establish." In biblical Hebrew, there are also variants and compounds. The fundamental image is that of the soil on which we depend, the territory that nourishes and where we take root.
H0776G.emploi: This word appears more than two thousand times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in Genesis and the historical books. At the beginning of the narrative, "earth" refers to the entirety of the created world (Genesis 1:1-2). Then the meaning becomes more precise: the land of Canaan becomes the divine promise to Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 12:1, Exodus 33:1). It can also evoke the experience of uprooting: Cain, cast out from the presence of God, becomes "a fugitive on the earth" (Genesis 4:14), meaning without anchor or refuge. The word's significance changes depending on the context: cosmic when it concerns creation, political when it concerns sovereignty, theological when it concerns the covenant.
H0776G.portee: This word reminds the believer that the earth is not an illusion or an accident, but a creation of God imbued with meaning. The promise of a land — Canaan for Israel — shows that God acts in concrete history, giving places, territories where faith can be lived out. It is also an invitation to consider our rooting: where are we called to live? For whom do we work? Finally, the contrast sometimes established between "earth" and heaven reminds us that this world is not our ultimate end, but the field where God accomplishes His purpose.

sens: the solid matter that makes up the globe
the soil, the surface where plants grow and living beings walk
a region, a country, a defined territory
the inhabitants of a region or country
the act of bowing down by touching the ground with one's forehead
H0776H.detail: 1. The earth in the sense of the entire globe, the whole of solid creation: "Let the earth bring forth living creatures" (Genesis 1:24) shows the earth as this created matter from which life springs. 2. The soil or terrestrial surface on which one walks, where cultivation occurs, where creeping animals crawl: "all the creeping things that creep on the earth" (Leviticus 11:42) specifically refers to the ground of creation. 3. A territory, a country, a region: "Carry away from the land what belongs to you" (Jeremiah 10:17) speaks of the territory where inhabitants live. 4. The people who inhabit a region: "people of the earth" means the inhabitants of a country, those who live there. 5. The act of bowing down, bending down to the ground, forehead to the soil: "he bowed down with his face to the ground" (2 Samuel 14:33) describes a gesture of respect or absolute submission.
H0776H.origine: The word comes from a fundamental Semitic root. Érez literally means "soil," "solid surface" — the starting image is that of firm ground underfoot, as opposed to heaven or water. It is a very ancient word in Semitic languages, evoking both physical matter and the idea of an inhabited land, a space for life.
H0776H.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Bible (180 occurrences). It primarily denotes physical creation: earth and heaven (Genesis 1). Very often, it signifies a territory or country — the land of Canaan, the land of Egypt, the land of Israel — with an emphasis on the inhabitants who live there. It can also refer to the ground where one places their feet, where one falls, where one bows down: it is a gesture of humility or respect. In lamentations or as a sign of mourning, one throws oneself to the ground. The word also encompasses the idea of "country" in its measurements and boundaries, and sometimes the peoples who inhabit it.
H0776H.portee: This word reminds the believer that God is the creator of all that is solid, stable, and visible. The promised land is the inheritance that God gives to His people. When one bows down with their face to the ground, they physically acknowledge their smallness before God and His absolute authority. It is also a word that anchors faith in the real, the concrete, the space where we live, where God acts.

sens: Chief of the royal house of King Ela of Israel
H0777.detail: Artsa is a character from the divided kingdom period, mentioned only once in Scripture. He served as chief of the royal house of King Ela of Israel, meaning he administered the palace and its servants (1 Kings 16:9). It was in his residence in Tirzah that King Ela was drinking when the conspirator Zimri assassinated him — a detail that underscores the intimacy of his role with the sovereign.
H0777.origine: The name Artsa means "earthly" or "of the earth" in Hebrew, formed from the root אֶרֶץ (eretz, "earth"). It is a typical descriptive name in ancient Hebrew vocabulary, where proper names often evoked a quality or trait.
H0777.emploi: Artsa appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 16:9, where he is referred to as "chief of the king's house." This was an important role: leading the royal house involved overseeing the palace, the servants, and the domestic affairs of the sovereign. It was during a feast likely held at his place, or at least under his roof, that the drama of Zimri's coup against King Ela unfolded.
H0777.portee: This brief passage reminds us that even the closest servants of kings — and the most important in the household — can do nothing against the divine will to change reigns. Artsa disappears from the text as quickly as he appears, a collateral victim of a royal conspiracy.

sens: The soil, the terrestrial matter on which one walks and cultivates
The entirety of solid land, continents and habitable surfaces, as opposed to waters
The created world, the visible universe with its inhabitants
Humanity and society that populate the earth
H0778.detail: 1. The earth is primarily the physical soil, the solid matter of the planet — the ground, the substance of plains and mountains. It is what one walks on, builds on, cultivates. 2. By extension, this word denotes all habitable lands, the terrestrial world as opposed to heaven: "The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth" (Jeremiah 10:11) — here "earth" represents all visible creation. 3. The earth can also evoke the inhabitants of this land, humanity and its activity: those who live, work, and turn to gods or to the true God. 4. Sometimes, the word takes on a moral or political hue: the earth as a domain of kingship, property, or as an issue of God's judgment.
H0778.origine: This Aramaic word (אֲרַק — araq) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word eretz (אֶרֶץ), which literally means "soil" or "earth." Both words share the same Semitic root, reflecting the initial idea of a solid surface, of firm matter. Aramaic was the language spoken by the Jews upon their return from exile, and this word has been preserved with the same fundamental meaning. In biblical Hebrew, eretz appears hundreds of times to denote soil, the promised land, or the inhabited world.
H0778.emploi: This Aramaic word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 10:11, the only verse in Aramaic of a prophecy otherwise in Hebrew. It is used twice in the same phrase: "The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from under the heavens." The first occurrence denotes the earth as part of creation (with heaven), and the second reinforces the idea by reminding that these false gods will completely fade away, even from the terrestrial surface. The context is one of critique of idols and affirmation of the power of the true Creator God. This unique passage shows that the word, even in Aramaic, retains all its biblical force.
H0778.portee: This verse reminds the believer that only the true God is the creator of the earth and the heavens — that all that exists is His work. It calls us to place our trust only in Him, not in idols or human powers that pass away. The spectacle of false gods disappearing from the earth is an invitation to faithfulness to the living God, who alone endures forever.

sens: To pronounce a curse against someone or something, calling misfortune upon them
To be struck by a curse, to suffer misfortune as punishment
To speak ill of someone, to criticize or insult them in words
To be declared cursed, rejected by God
H0779.detail:
1. To curse is to solemnly pronounce a word of misfortune against a person or thing. The serpent is cursed by God (Genesis 3:14): God declares that it will henceforth be the most despised creature, condemned to crawl on its belly. It is an official divine word that changes destiny.

2. To be cursed means to receive this curse, to bear misfortune within oneself. The children of Israel who disobey will see their fruits cursed, their harvests struck with barrenness (Deuteronomy 28:18). The curse is not just a word: it is a reality that falls upon what is cursed.

3. To curse someone also means to speak words of insult or anger to them. The Lord forbids Moses from cursing the magistrates of the people (Exodus 22:28). Balaam, the diviner, is hired to curse Israel in words (Numbers 23:7).

4. When the Bible says that something is cursed, it means that it is rejected by God, marked by His opposition. Whoever lies with a beast must be cursed (Deuteronomy 27:21), meaning solemnly excluded from the covenant community.
H0779.origine: The Hebrew root אָרַר (arar) denotes the act of cursing, of pronouncing a word of misfortune. It is linked to the idea of pushing away, rejecting forcefully. In biblical Hebrew, the verb has several forms: the simple form expresses the action of cursing, while the passive form means to be cursed. The word is rooted in experience: a curse is a powerful word that changes the course of events, especially when it comes from God or a recognized authority.
H0779.emploi: This verb appears about 52 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Law and the accounts of blessing/curse. The usages are concentrated in three areas: first, Genesis, where the curse of the serpent opens the series of the world's misfortunes (Genesis 3:14); then Deuteronomy, which lists the curses that strike those who violate the covenant (Deuteronomy 27-28); finally, in the historical and prophetic books, where individuals or acts are declared cursed. The meaning remains constant: it is always a word that expresses divine rejection or hostility toward someone. In Balaam's case, to curse is the opposite of blessing: he is asked to "curse Jacob" (Numbers 23:7), but he can only bless him. In the Deuteronomic prescriptions, the curses extend to crops, animals, and the children of the one who transgresses.
H0779.portee: The word to curse confronts the reader with the reality of divine judgment. When God curses something or someone, it is never arbitrary: it is always in reaction to rebellion, sin, or transgression of the covenant. This reminds us that our actions have consequences, that God is holy, and that sin does not go unanswered. But it is also a call to wisdom: not to act in a way that attracts a curse upon oneself. For the Christian, this highlights how Jesus, by taking upon Himself the curse due to our sins (Galatians 3:13), has freed us from this condemnation.

sens: Mountainous region of the ancient Near East where Noah's ark came to rest
Kingdom or territory of the ancient world known for its warriors and horses
H0780.detail:
1. Ararat is a mountainous region located between the Araxes River and the Van and Urmia lakes, in eastern present-day Armenia. It is where Noah's ark came to rest after the flood: "In the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat" (Genesis 8:4). This place marks the moment when humanity begins anew after the catastrophe of the flood.
2. Ararat also becomes the name of a kingdom or warrior region of the ancient Near East, capable of mobilizing fighters and horses for battle. When the prophet Jeremiah must announce judgment against Babylon, he cries out: "Call against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz!" (Jeremiah 51:27), listing them among the military powers that God raises up.
H0780.origine: The Hebrew name אֲרָרַט (Ararat) designates the mountain range of southern Caucasus. Its exact etymology remains debated, but it refers to a real and well-identified geographical region in antiquity, known to the peoples of the Levant. The name appears in ancient cuneiform texts in related forms, confirming its grounding in the history of the Near East.
H0780.emploi: The word Ararat appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the sense of a region or territorial power. In Genesis 8:4, it first designates the place of the ark's resting after the flood. Then, in the parallel accounts of 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38, it appears as a refuge region where the assassins of the Assyrian king Sennacherib flee. Finally, in Jeremiah 51:27, it is mentioned among the kingdoms that God summons to judge Babylon, alongside Minni and Ashkenaz. Its meaning remains geographical and political: it is always a reality of the ancient world visible and known to biblical readers.
H0780.portee: Ararat reminds the reader that the flood did not annihilate humanity: the ark found an anchor point, and a new story could begin. It is a place of salvation and new creation. Furthermore, its mention among the powers that God commands to rise shows that the Lord masters the kingdoms of the world and directs them according to His plan of judgment and redemption.

sens: To establish a marriage engagement between a man and a woman
To solemnly promise someone in marriage
To bind by a promise of marital union
H0781.detail:
1. The verb to betroth means to seal an official marriage engagement: a man and a woman promise themselves to each other before living together. It is the legal and social act that precedes the actual marriage. In Exodus 22:16, a man who seduces a virgin who is not betrothed must take her as his wife, which implies formally betrothing her.
2. To betroth also describes the state of one who is bound by this engagement: a betrothed young girl is promised to someone and belongs only to him. In Deuteronomy 22:23, a betrothed virgin is not yet married, but she is already reserved, and violating this bond is a serious crime.
3. The term evokes the image of a solemn and binding promise, which creates rights and duties between the two families. This engagement gives the betrothed a special status and legal protection.
H0781.origine: The Hebrew verb אָרַשׂ (aras) comes from a root meaning "to attach," "to bind," or "to engage." The family of words evokes the idea of creating a strong and lasting bond. The word appears in the legal and familial contexts of the Old Testament to describe this marital engagement which, in Israelite culture, was a solemn act with the force of law.
H0781.emploi: This verb appears ten times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in legal and matrimonial contexts. It is found mainly in Deuteronomy (5 times), where the Law establishes the rights and protections of betrothed virgins: Deuteronomy 20:7 exempted from the army the man who had just betrothed a woman; Deuteronomy 22:23-27 distinguishes the punishments based on whether the violated woman was betrothed or not. The word also appears in 2 Samuel 3:14, where Michal remembers her betrothal to David. In Hosea 2:21-22, the prophet uses the image of betrothal to describe the renewed covenant between God and Israel: "I will betroth you to me in righteousness." The term always marks an official engagement recognized by law.
H0781.portee: Understanding biblical betrothal sheds light on the serious commitment represented by the marital promise in the Christian faith. It is a strong bond, creating duties and rights, not a vague or provisional relationship. The image that Hosea borrows — God betrothing Himself to His people — shows that the divine covenant is as unshakeable and personal as a marriage commitment. For the believer, this reminds us that the promises exchanged before God deserve respect and fidelity.

sens: What one wishes to obtain
Desire expressed in words
H0782.detail:
1. What one wishes to obtain: the word evokes a need or a vow that one formulates. In Psalms 21:3, "what his lips requested" speaks of what a person expresses as a wish or request.
2. Desire expressed in words: the request is not silent; it is spoken, it comes out of the mouth. It is a desire that takes shape in words to be presented to someone.
H0782.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to seek," "to desire." It denotes the act of asking something from someone, often in a context of prayer or a request addressed to God. The word is essential: one asks by speaking, which is why the text mentions "the lips."
H0782.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 21:3, it describes what the king desires and expresses through his words: God granted him "what his lips requested." The context is one of praise directed to the king, celebrating the fulfillment of his vows. It is a word that belongs to the realm of prayer and request.
H0782.portee: This passage reminds us that God hears the requests that spring from the heart and mouth of those who trust Him. It is an invitation to openly express our desires and needs to God, with the certainty that He listens and can grant what we ask.

sens: King of Persia, son and successor of Xerxes, who reigned from 465 to 424 B.C.
H0783A.detail: Artaxerxes is a Persian king who played a crucial role in the history of Israel during the return from exile. It was under his reign that the prophet Ezra went up from Babylon to Jerusalem to restore the divine Law among the people (Ezra 7:1). The king even granted him an official letter authorizing this mission and providing him with resources from the royal treasury (Ezra 7:11). Nehemiah, governor of Judah, also served this king as the cupbearer before obtaining permission from him to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:1).
H0783A.origine: The name Artaxerxes is of Persian origin. According to tradition, its meaning is related to the idea of greatness and royal power. Historically, it refers to Artaxerxes I, the son and successor of King Xerxes, who expanded and consolidated the Persian Empire in the 5th century B.C.
H0783A.emploi: Artaxerxes is mentioned 8 times in the Bible, all in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which cover the return of the exiles from Babylon. The first mention is found in Ezra 4:7, where adversaries write to the king to oppose the rebuilding of the temple. Later, both Ezra and Nehemiah receive letters and authorizations from the king to carry out their respective missions (Ezra 7:1-11 and Nehemiah 2:1). These references show how God used a pagan king to facilitate the restoration of His people and worship.
H0783A.portee: The story of Artaxerxes illustrates how God governs the hearts of kings and accomplishes His plans even through unlikely instruments. The decrees of the Persian king allowed for the reconstruction of the temple and the walls of Jerusalem, thus fulfilling the promises of divine restoration. For the believer, this teaches that no earthly power can hinder the work of God.

sens: King of Persia who reigned from 465 to 424 B.C.
Successor of Xerxes at the head of the Persian Empire
H0783B.detail: Artaxerxes is a Persian king mentioned in the book of Ezra as the sovereign who authorized the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem and supported Ezra in his religious mission. He received letters from the governors established in Trans-Euphrates, pleading with him to stop the reconstruction of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:8-11); he then ordered the cessation of the work (Ezra 4:23). However, his reign also saw the completion of the temple, whose construction continued according to the order of the God of Israel and the successive decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes (Ezra 6:14). Later, he granted Ezra the priest and scribe extensive powers to enforce the law of God and provided considerable resources to the royal treasurers (Ezra 7:12, 7:21).
H0783B.origine: The name Artaxerxes, of Persian origin, literally means "I will make the spoiled boil; I will stir in winter" according to ancient etymology, although this translation is more of an interpretative attempt than the true meaning of the royal Persian name. It is a dynastic title held by several monarchs of the Achaemenid Persia. The text of Ezra uses the Aramaic form of the name, the administrative language of the Persian Empire.
H0783B.emploi: Artaxerxes appears six times in the book of Ezra, all in chapters 4, 6, and 7, which cover the post-exilic period. Initially, he is the recipient of a letter from local governors pleading with him to block the reconstruction of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:8, 4:11), to which he consents by ordering the work to stop (Ezra 4:23). Later, his name appears alongside those of Cyrus and Darius in the decree authorizing the completion of the temple (Ezra 6:14). Finally, in chapters 7 and following, he is presented as the monarch who grants Ezra the authority to reform the religious and civil life of the Jews returned from exile, entrusting him with substantial royal resources (Ezra 7:12, 7:21).
H0783B.portee: Artaxerxes embodies the paradoxical role of worldly powers in God's plan: although he initially yielded to pressure to stop the construction of the temple, he ultimately contributed to its completion and supported the spiritual restoration project of Israel. His story shows how God governs earthly kingdoms to fulfill His purposes for His people.

sens: natural element that burns and produces heat and light
visible flames of a fire or hearth
fire for cooking or roasting food
altar fire for sacrifices
brilliant and terrible divine manifestation
anger of God
H0784.detail:
1. Fire is the element that burns and gives off heat and light: it is the material fire that everyone knows, used in homes and sacrifices. In Genesis 15:17, during the covenant with Abram, a smoking furnace and flames pass between the divided animals: this is ordinary fire, but here it manifests the divine presence.
2. The flames refer to the visible tongues of fire, its most striking aspect: these are the flames that consume and shine. The fire at Sinai in Exodus 19:18 rises like the smoke of a furnace, with spectacular flames.
3. The fire for cooking or roasting is that of meals: in Exodus 12:8-9, the Passover lamb must be roasted over the fire, and in Leviticus 2:14, the roasted ears of grain are an offering. It is the useful and everyday fire.
4. The altar fire is the sacred fire that consumes the sacrifices: it burns continually on the altar (Leviticus 1:7-8, Leviticus 9:24). It is a divine fire that manifests God's acceptance of the sacrifice.
5. Fire manifests God Himself in His majestic and terrifying theophanies: it surrounds God, revealing His holiness and power. In Exodus 3:2, the bush burns but is not consumed, showing the presence of the living God.
6. The anger of God is depicted by fire: in Numbers 11:1, when the people complain, the anger of the Lord burned, and the fire of the Lord blazed among them. Fire becomes the image of divine judgment, of the righteous indignation that consumes the sinner.
H0784.origine: The Hebrew word אֵשׁ (esh) is very ancient and simply designates fire in its primary sense. The root evokes the action of burning and consuming. This word is also known in Aramaic (אֶשָּׁא, escha). In the Bible, fire is omnipresent as a symbol: it is both life (heat, cooking, light), sacrifice (the consumed offering), and judgment (the divine anger that destroys). Fire is one of the favorite images of the Bible to speak of God and His action in history.
H0784.emploi: The word "fire" appears 348 times in the Old Testament, making it a fundamental term. It primarily designates material fire: the fire of the hearth, the fire for roasting the Passover, the fire of sacrifices at the Lord's altar (very frequent in Leviticus and Numbers). But it also takes on a spiritual meaning: it is the fire of the theophany, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:18) or in the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), which manifests the presence and fearsome holiness of God. Finally, fire represents divine anger and judgment: in Numbers 11:1, the fire of the Lord consumes the rebellious camp; in Ezekiel 15:7, the fire will consume those who have escaped. The context determines whether the fire is beneficial (cooking, accepted sacrifice) or destructive (judgment, anger).
H0784.portee: Fire in the Bible reminds the reader that God is a living and active God, who manifests Himself in tangible and sometimes fearsome ways. The altar fire teaches that the sacrifice purifies and that God accepts the believer's offering. But fire is also a call to respect divine holiness: those who approach God lightly (like Nadab and Abihu in Leviticus 10:1-2) are consumed. For the Christian, the fire of God reveals both His goodness that purifies and His judgment that destroys sin.

sens: Element that burns and consumes
H0785.detail: 1. Fire is the physical element that consumes and destroys: in Daniel's vision, the monstrous beast is delivered to the fire to be annihilated (Daniel 7:11). It is an image of total and irreversible destruction.
H0785.origine: This Aramaic word אֶשָּׁא (eshsha) is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word אֵשׁ (esh), both meaning fire. Aramaic and Hebrew share the same Semitic roots, and this term simply designates the natural element of combustion. The word is also used figuratively to speak of divine anger or judgment.
H0785.emploi: This word appears only once in Aramaic in the New Testament, in Daniel's prophetic vision in chapter 7. It is a symbolic vision where Daniel sees beasts representing the kingdoms of men, and the last one is judged: its body is delivered to the fire to be destroyed. This fire of divine judgment foreshadows God's final justice.
H0785.portee: Fire in this passage symbolizes God's justice that destroys evil and injustice. This image teaches the reader that despite the apparent power of human kingdoms and their arrogant claims, God maintains absolute control and judges according to His justice. Fire consumes what is contrary to His will.

sens: absence of something
nonexistence
nothing of what is stated
H0786.detail:
1. The word expresses complete absence, nothingness: in 2 Samuel 14:19, the woman swears that there is "nothing" to the right or left of what the king commands — that is, she has omitted nothing, hidden nothing, forgotten nothing of his words.
2. It can also designate what no longer exists or does not yet exist, the absence of an expected reality: in Micah 6:10, the prophet ironically asks if there are "still" any unjust treasures — the absence of limit, of honesty, in the house of the wicked.
H0786.origine: This Hebrew word is an adverbial form that expresses absence or nonexistence. It is related to the notion of emptiness, of what is not. In the Hebrew Bible, it serves to deny the existence or presence of something, often in a question or solemn statement.
H0786.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible according to the provided usages. In 2 Samuel 14:19, it affirms the total absence of omission or falsehood — the servant swears by the king's life that she has hidden nothing. In Micah 6:10, it expresses the absence or moral insufficiency, the rhetorical question of the prophet denouncing the absence of justice in the wicked. These two contexts show how nothingness can signify both material absence and absence of righteousness.
H0786.portee: This word reminds us that truth before God requires total transparency — nothing should be hidden or withheld. It also highlights how the absence of justice and righteousness characterizes one who opposes God: the wicked is empty of what constitutes the essence of good.

sens: The stone or masonry bases on which a building is raised
That on which the religious or civil edifice rests, the principle of stability
H0787.detail:
1. The word designates the material foundations of a house or temple: the underground structures of stone or brick that support the entire edifice. In Ezra 5:16, Zerubbabel "laid the foundations of the house of God" — this refers to the concrete act of digging and laying the first stones of the Temple rebuilt after the exile.
2. In a broader sense, "foundation" means the principle or solid base on which a lasting reality rests. In Ezra 6:3, King Cyrus orders that the house be rebuilt "with solid foundations," expressing the desire that the Temple be established in a stable and enduring manner, worthy of its role in worship.
H0787.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew root אָשְׁיָה (ashyah), which means "foundation." It belongs to the vocabulary of construction and architecture. Its original meaning is very concrete: the stones or structure that are first laid to support all that will be built upon it.
H0787.emploi: The word appears three times in the book of Ezra, always in the context of the reconstruction of the Temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (circa 538-515 B.C.). In Ezra 4:12, the adversaries of the Jews mention the rebuilding of the walls and the restoration of the foundations as a sign of the city's renewal. In Ezra 5:16, it is reported that Zerubbabel, the governor appointed by Cyrus, laid the foundations of the Temple. In Ezra 6:3, the royal decree stipulates that the house be rebuilt on solid foundations. The word is thus always linked to the concrete action of building and the idea of solidity.
H0787.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the importance of a solid foundation: spiritually, as physically, what endures must be based on stable principles. The reconstruction of the Temple after the exile speaks of restoration and renewal, a sign of God's faithfulness to His people even in trial.

sens: Son of Benjamin
Ancestor of a Benjaminite family
H0788.detail:
1. Aschbel is a son of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogy of the tribes of Israel. He is presented as the second son of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:1), among a sibling group of ten brothers: Bela, Beker, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard (Genesis 46:21).
2. As an ancestor of a clan, Aschbel gives his name to the family of the Aschbelites (Numbers 26:38), one of the families of the tribe of Benjamin. In each census of the people, this family is counted among the Benjamites.
H0788.origine: The name Aschbel may mean "man in God" or "fire of Bel" according to ancient interpretations. It is composed of Hebrew elements; "bel" possibly evokes the divine name or a notion of power. Aschbel is a typical name in the genealogies of the Old Testament that connects each person to their founding ancestor.
H0788.emploi: Aschbel is a genealogical figure who appears three times in Scripture: in Genesis 46:21 during the list of Benjamin's sons going down to Egypt; in 1 Chronicles 8:1 where he is named as the second son; and in Numbers 26:38 where his descendants are counted as one of the Benjaminite families. His name only appears in these genealogical lists; there are no personal accounts detailing his actions. He simply represents a branch of the tribe of Benjamin, founding an identifiable clan during the censuses.

sens: Descendants of Aschbel, son of Benjamin
H0789.detail: 1. The Aschbelites are the members of the family clan that descends from Aschbel, one of the sons of Benjamin. This name refers not to the person of Aschbel himself, but to his descendants, those who belong to his lineage and carry his genealogical heritage.
H0789.origine: The word "Aschbelites" is formed from the name of Aschbel, son of Benjamin, with the usual suffix meaning "descendants of" or "those who belong to." Aschbel first appears during the census of Jacob's sons in Egypt (Genesis 46:21), and his descendants are attested during the second census in the wilderness.
H0789.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:38, during the census of the families of Benjamin in the wilderness of Sinai. It is an administrative and genealogical term: it serves to identify the members of Aschbel's clan among the people of Israel, alongside the Balites, the Achiramites, and other Benjaminite families. This census is part of the preparation of the people before entering the promised land.

sens: Man of the descendants of Edom during the Patriarchs' time
H0790.detail: Eschban is a minor character in the Bible, mentioned only twice. He is a son of Dishon, himself a descendant of Edom, the brother of Esau. He appears in the genealogy of the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:26) and is listed among the brothers Hemdan, Jithran, and Karen.
H0790.origine: The name Eschban means "fire of discernment" in Hebrew. It appears in the genealogies of Edom preserved in Genesis and repeated in 1 Chronicles, reflecting the importance of genealogical lists for ancient families of the Near East.
H0790.emploi: Eschban is mentioned only twice in the Bible: in Genesis 36:26 and in 1 Chronicles 1:41. He appears in the genealogical lists of the descendants of Dishon, a chief of Edom. These enumerations served to establish lineages and the rights of tribal leaders. He is a character from patriarchal history without a particular narrative role, known only by his belonging to a notable Edomite family.

sens: Ancestor of a family of Judah
H0791.detail: Aschbéa is the patriarch of a family that descends from Shelah, himself a son of Judah. The text of 1 Chronicles 4:21 mentions him as the head of a house or lineage famous for the work of fine linen, a precious fabric used notably in priestly garments.
H0791.origine: The name means "I will make swear" and combines the element "Beth" (בַּיִת, "house") with a verb expressing the idea of covenant or oath. It designates a founding ancestor of a lineage recognizable by his trade.
H0791.emploi: Aschbéa appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:21, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as a patriarch whose house was renowned for the textile industry of fine linen, suggesting a family of notable social and economic status in the history of the people of Israel.

sens: Son of Saul, king of Israel during the united monarchy
H0792.detail: Eschbaal is the fourth son of King Saul. He is also known by the name Ishbosheth, which the Bible primarily uses in the account of 2 Samuel. His other name, Eschbaal, appears in the genealogical lists of 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39, which enumerate the descendants of Saul. These two names refer to the same person: "Eschbaal" literally means "man of Baal" in Hebrew, while "Ishbosheth" uses "bosheth" (shame) to replace the name of the god Baal, in order to avoid pronouncing this pagan name — a common practice in later biblical texts.
H0792.origine: The name Eschbaal is composed of two elements: "esch" ("ish"), which means "man," and "Baal," the name of the fertility god worshiped by the Canaanite peoples. This name likely reflects the religious practices of the time of Saul. Ishbosheth, his other name, replaces Baal with "bosheth" (shame), which shows the respect that later writers had for the name of the true God by rejecting references to other deities.
H0792.emploi: Eschbaal appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the same repeated passage of 1 Chronicles (8:33 and 9:39), where he is listed in the genealogy of Saul among his four sons. The account in 2 Samuel systematically uses the name Ishbosheth for the same person, notably in 2 Samuel 2-4, where he is presented as a rival king after Saul's death, before being assassinated. The use of these two names in the Bible shows how the genealogies of 1 Chronicles preserve the older name (Eschbaal) while the narrative account of 2 Samuel uses the revised name (Ishbosheth) to avoid pronouncing the name of the god Baal.

sens: bed or course of a stream
region traversed by a stream
lower part of a valley
H0793.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the course of a stream, that is, the bed through which the waters flow. In Numbers 21:15, it refers to the "course of the torrents" that extends in the region of Ar, at the border of Moab: it is the valley or the path carved by the torrents in the rocky terrain of the desert.
2. By extension, the word can also designate the region traversed by these torrents, the ravines and mountain valleys that water has carved over time.
3. The meaning aligns with that of "lower part" or "bottom," as the course of the torrents is always down below, in the hollows of the terrain.
H0793.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of descending and flowing downward. This is why it naturally describes the beds of waterways, where water cascades down slopes. The same word can mean "slope" or "hillside," as one thinks of the movement of water flowing downward.
H0793.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 21:15. It designates the course of a torrent, an element of the desert landscape in the region of Moab. Its unique use in the biblical text shows that it is a precise term for describing the geography of the Arabian desert, the torrents that carve through rocky valleys.
H0793.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks of real and concrete places. In Numbers 21, Moses enumerates the borders of the Promised Land by mentioning the features of the terrain: the torrents and their courses are not poetic details, but the actual landmarks of the territory that God gives to His people.

sens: Gentle slope of a mountain or hill
Geographical region characterized by this rugged relief
H0794.detail:
1. A hill is a gentle slope that descends from a height. It is less steep than a rugged mountain but more uneven than a flat plain. In Joshua 10:40, when Joshua "struck all the land, the hill country, the Negev, the lowland, and the hills," the term refers to these intermediate relief areas that characterized the terrain of Canaan.
2. By extension, "the hills" become a region or geographical area defined by this type of terrain. In Joshua 12:8, when the text lists "the hill country, the valley, the lowland, the hills, the desert, and the Negev," it describes the different regions that Joshua conquered based on their topography.
H0794.origine: The Hebrew word אֲשֵׁדָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of slope or inclination. It literally designates land that "descends" or "inclines." This word belongs to the geographical vocabulary of the Bible and is used to describe the characteristics of the soil and relief.
H0794.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Joshua (10:40 and 12:8). In these two passages, it is part of a list of the different geographical areas of Canaan: hill country, valley, lowland, hills, desert, and Negev. These lists show how Joshua systematically conquered all the territory, regardless of its topography. The word fits into the description of the Palestinian relief as seen by the ancient Israelites.
H0794.portee: This word reminds us that Joshua's victory was total and without exception: it covered all the terrain, from the highest to the lowest, from the most rugged to the flattest. This underscores the completeness of God's promise and the reality of His power that extends to every aspect of the conquered territory.

sens: Major Philistine city on the Mediterranean coast
Religious and political center of the Philistines
Symbol of pagan power opposed to Israel
H0795.detail:
1. Ashdod is one of the five main Philistine cities, located on the Mediterranean coast west of Jerusalem. It is an important and fortified urban center, with walls, temples, and surrounding territory (Joshua 15:47).

2. It is a significant Philistine religious site, notably the seat of the temple of the god Dagon. When the Ark of the Covenant was brought there, the inhabitants recognized the power of the God of Israel through the plagues that struck the city and its god (1 Samuel 5:5, 5:7).

3. In prophecies, Ashdod represents the enemy power of foreign nations opposed to God; it is often mentioned alongside other Philistine cities as a symbol of the pagan world that the Lord will judge (Jeremiah 25:20).
H0795.origine: The name means "mighty" in Hebrew, reflecting the strategic and military importance of this city. Ashdod was indeed one of the five main cities of the Philistines, a people who controlled the Palestinian coast before the Israelite conquest.
H0795.emploi: Ashdod appears about fifteen times in the Bible, primarily in the historical accounts of the conquest and the Israeli-Philistine conflict (Joshua, 1 Samuel), and then in the prophecies of judgment against the nations (Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah, Zechariah). It is always presented as a stronghold of military and religious power, sometimes mentioned as a center of resistance to the Israelites, and at other times as a target of divine judgment. Its temple of Dagon is particularly associated with manifestations of the power of the God of Israel (1 Samuel 5).
H0795.portee: Ashdod reminds the reader that even the most powerful and well-established cities—with their walls, temples, and gods—cannot withstand the living God. Its history illustrates that true power does not reside in human fortifications, but in obedience to God.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Ashdod
Philistine from Ashdod
Enemy of Israel established in Philistia
H0796.detail:
1. The term designates an inhabitant or member of the people established in the city of Ashdod, one of the five great cities of ancient Philistia. This coastal city was an important center of Philistine power, as seen in Joshua 13:3 where Ashdod is mentioned among the Philistine principalities.

2. The Ashdodites are presented as Philistines, that is, the inhabitants of the maritime region of Canaan called Philistia. In 1 Samuel 5:3, the Ashdodites discover the statue of their god Dagon overturned before the Ark of the Lord, which shows their religious and military character in relation to Israel.

3. In the biblical accounts, the Ashdodites appear as adversaries of Israel: in 1 Samuel 5:6, the Lord strikes the Ashdodites with a divine plague, and in Nehemiah 4:7 and 13:23, they oppose the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the religious reforms of God's people.
H0796.origine: The word comes from the name of the city of Ashdod (אַשְׁדּוֹד), one of the five main Philistine cities on the Canaanite coast. The suffix -י (-i) in Hebrew creates an adjective or a people name from the place name, a common formation to designate the inhabitants of a city or region. Ashdod itself was a center of worship for the god Dagon and a strategic port on the eastern Mediterranean.
H0796.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the accounts of conflicts between Israel and Philistia. In Joshua 13:3, it is included in the enumeration of Philistine territories not yet conquered. The major usage is found in 1 Samuel 5, where the Ashdodites experience the power of the Lord through the divine judgment that strikes their city after the capture of the Ark (verses 3 and 6). Later, in Nehemiah 4:7 and 13:23, the Ashdodites reappear as opponents to the restoration of Jerusalem and as a threat to the religious purity of Israel through mixed marriages. The context always shows tension or hostility with God's people.
H0796.portee: These accounts teach that the power of foreign nations and their gods is limited before the God of Israel. The Lord's victory over Dagon and the plague sent to the Ashdodites illustrate God's superiority. More broadly, the Ashdodite opposition in Nehemiah reminds us that God's people always face external and internal resistances, but that faithfulness to God and His commandments remains the path to victory.

sens: Inhabitant of Ashdod
H0797.detail: The term designates the inhabitants or descendants of the inhabitants of Ashdod, a major Philistine city on the Mediterranean coast. It refers here to a people with distinct characteristics, notably their own language.
H0797.origine: It is the demonym derived from Ashdod, one of the five major Philistine cities. The name Ashdod means "I will devastate" in ancient Hebrew. In Nehemiah, the text refers to the "Ashdodite language," showing that this people had its own well-established linguistic and cultural identity.
H0797.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 13:24, where it designates the language spoken by the inhabitants of Ashdod. Nehemiah observes with concern that some Jewish children have married Ashdodite women and no longer speak Hebrew, but rather the language of their mothers. This passage illustrates the tensions between Jewish identity and the influences of neighboring pagan peoples, especially in the post-exilic period.
H0797.portee: This term reminds the reader how contamination through alliances with surrounding nations threatens the spiritual and cultural identity of Israel. It serves as a warning against assimilation that diverts the people from their roots and faith.

sens: Mountain range to the east of the Jordan, where Mount Nebo is located
H0798.detail: 1. Pisgah is a mountainous region located on the eastern bank of the Jordan, in Transjordan. The word literally means "slopes" or "hillsides," which evokes the steep sides of this mountain range. It is here that Moses ascends to view the Promised Land before he dies (Deuteronomy 34:1-4), and the region is geographically defined in the descriptions of Israel's borders: it forms the southern boundary of the lands given to the tribes of Reuben and Gad, at the foot of which lies the plain (Deuteronomy 3:17; Deuteronomy 4:49).
H0798.origine: The Hebrew word אַשְׁדּוֹת (ashdoth) properly means "slopes" or "hillsides" (from the root שׁדד, suggesting the idea of descent). It is always used in the Bible in combination with "Pisgah" (פִּסְגָּה), forming the geographical name "Ashdoth-Pisgah" or simply "Pisgah." This region is also referred to as the "mountains of Pisgah," and it notably includes Mount Nebo, from which Moses gazes upon the Promised Land.
H0798.emploi: Pisgah appears four times in the historical and geographical texts of the Bible, always to designate a boundary or territorial landmark in Transjordan. In Deuteronomy (3:17 and 4:49), Moses describes the lands he distributes to the tribes of Reuben and Gad: Pisgah marks the southern limit, at the foot of which lies the Jordan plain. In the book of Joshua (12:3 and 13:20), during the conquest, the region of Pisgah is again mentioned as a boundary marker, still to the south of the Transjordanian lands. It is a fixed point in biblical geography, both for delineating inheritances and for recounting Moses' final act.

sens: Shelter or enclosure where domestic animals are fed, especially horses and cattle
Space arranged to store or keep farm animals
H0723.detail:
1. A manger is a shelter, a building, or an enclosure specifically designed to house and feed domestic animals. It is a place where they are kept safe and fed. Solomon, the king of Israel, had forty thousand for his war horses and chariots (1 Kings 4:26).
2. The word more broadly refers to any space intended to keep livestock — horses, donkeys, oxen, sheep. Solomon built mangers for all the animals he accumulated, a sign of his royal wealth (2 Chronicles 32:28).
H0723.origine: The Hebrew word אֻרְיָה (uriah) derives from a root that evokes the idea of eating or grazing. It is related to the word אֲוֵרָה (aveah) which has the same meaning. The word paints the image of a place of nourishment: it is where animals are fed, where they find their pasture, hence the name 'manger'.
H0723.emploi: This word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the historical books (1 Kings and 2 Chronicles), and always to describe Solomon's royal facilities. It refers to the buildings where the king stored and fed his horses — an enormous wealth: forty thousand mangers for forty thousand horses (1 Kings 4:26), then four thousand mangers in 2 Chronicles 9:25. The context shows that these mangers represented considerable economic power, a symbol of the magnificence of this king.
H0723.portee: This word reminds us that Solomon's wealth was not only in gold or wisdom, but also in very concrete resources — horses, livestock, land, and buildings. It is a detail that humanizes the narrative and shows the material scope of a biblical kingdom.

sens: Restoration of physical health or well-being
Repair, reconstruction of a damaged structure
Moral or spiritual restoration, reestablishment of a state of peace
H0724.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the healing of an illness or injury: the return to health. In Jeremiah 8:22, the prophet asks why 'the healing of the daughter of my people does not take place?', meaning why the people do not regain their vitality. It is a restoration of the body or the whole person.
2. The word is also used for the material repair of buildings or structures: in 2 Chronicles 24:13, it speaks of the 'repair' of the temple, meaning its reconstruction after damage. In Nehemiah 4:7, it refers to the 'repair' of the walls of Jerusalem being restored stone by stone.
3. In a spiritual and metaphorical sense, it is the restoration of peace and trust. In Jeremiah 33:6, God promises 'healing and health' with 'an abundant source of peace and faithfulness': it is the return to a state of grace and reconciliation with God after disaster.
H0724.origine: The word comes from a root that means 'to become whole, to recover'. It evokes the idea of regaining form, becoming complete again after a break or fracture. Words from the same family describe what is 'whole', 'intact', or 'complete'. This is why the term covers both physical healing and material repair: in both cases, it is about restoring something to its lost integrity.
H0724.emploi: This word appears 6 times in biblical Hebrew, mostly in the prophets and historical books. It is used for the healing of the body in Jeremiah 30:17 ('I will heal you, I will bind up your wounds') and Isaiah 58:8 ('your healing shall spring forth speedily'). It also refers to the repair of buildings: the temple in 2 Chronicles 24:13, the walls of Jerusalem in Nehemiah 4:7. In each context, it is a process of restoration: return to health, physical reconstruction, or reconciliation and spiritual peace with God.
H0724.portee: Healing is never an accident in the Bible: it is always an act of God who restores, repairs, and lifts up. For the believer, this means that God does not merely punish or destroy — He restores and heals. The word invites trust: God can bind up wounds and make whole what is broken, physically and spiritually.

sens: Fortified place near Shechem, in Canaan
H0725.detail: Aruma is a city or small town located near Shechem, in the Promised Land. It is where Abimelech withdrew after conquering and destroying Shechem (Judges 9:41): while Zebul drives out the insurgent Gaal and his brothers from the city, Abimelech waits in this fortified refuge, from where he can direct his operations.
H0725.origine: The Hebrew name ערוּמָה (Aruma) literally means 'that which will be elevated' or 'exalted', from the root that evokes elevation or height. It is a typical place name of the Levant, often given to fortified places or those on heights. The name also appears in the form Rumah.
H0725.emploi: Aruma appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 9:41. The account in the book of Judges reports Abimelech's rebellion against the city of Shechem: after crushing the revolt led by Gaal, Abimelech withdraws to Aruma, a fortified place where he can maintain control of the region without directly occupying Shechem. This geographical detail shows how Abimelech consolidated his power in central Canaan during the time of the Judges.

sens: Chest or box made of wood, intended to contain precious objects or burial remains
Golden chest containing the tablets of the Law, symbol of the divine presence at the heart of Israelite worship
Sacred object that guides the people of Israel in their movements and battles
Container of the most holy elements of the sanctuary
H0727.detail:
1. In the simplest sense, an ark is a wooden chest serving as a receptacle: Joseph is placed 'in a coffin' in Egypt (Genesis 50:26), and the golden chest contained precious objects (1 Samuel 6:15). It is an object for transport and preservation.
2. The Ark of the Covenant is the specific chest built for the sanctuary: Moses makes 'an ark of acacia wood' (Deuteronomy 10:3) to place the stone tablets of the Law inside. It measures 2.5 cubits long and contains the ten commandments engraved.
3. This ark is not just a piece of furniture: it embodies the very presence of God among the people. When Joshua faces 'the ark of the Lord' (Joshua 7:6), he is not looking at just an object, but the visible sign of divine power. The Levites carry it during the movements of the camp and conquests (1 Chronicles 15:27).
4. In solemn processions, especially at the crossing of the Jordan and the siege of Jericho, the ark goes before the people, signaling that God Himself guides their march: it is never just a relic, but the point of contact between heaven and earth.
H0727.origine: The Hebrew word אֲרוֹן (aron) comes from a root that evokes the idea of 'to fit together' or 'to enclose'. It designates any container or chest, whether made of wood or stone. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), it is translated as 'arcē' (ἀρχή), but it is primarily a common word in domestic and cultic vocabulary. The same root appears in Arabic and Akkadian with the generic meaning of box or chest.
H0727.emploi: The word appears 174 times, concentrated in the texts of the Torah (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and historical books (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles). Almost all uses refer to the Ark of the Covenant: it is constructed (Exodus 25:10), transported (Joshua 3:3 to 4:18), venerated (1 Samuel 4:3-5), captured by the Philistines (1 Samuel 5:1-10), and then returned. The ark becomes the heart of Israelite worship: it represents the invisible throne of God and the place where His Word (the tablets of the Law) rests.
H0727.portee: The Ark of the Covenant reminds the believer that God does not remain distant or abstract, but establishes His presence at the very heart of His people: it is the concrete sign that the Lord walks with Israel and protects it. For the Christian reader, it foreshadows Christ, who will fully embody this divine presence. Finally, the sacred respect shown to the ark reminds us that the Word of God and His presence require reverence and worship.

sens: Region of the ancient Near East, north of the Promised Land
Powerful political kingdom, rival and enemy of Israel
People and nation of the Syrians
The gods worshiped in Syria, objects of idolatrous worship
H0758I.detail:
1. Syria is a geographical region of the Near East, located to the north and northeast of the Promised Land, with its capital being Damascus. It encompasses the Aramean kingdoms that were established there.
2. On several occasions, Syria forms a powerful kingdom that comes into conflict with Israel and Judah: Ben-Hadad and his successors wage wars against the Israelite kings, as when "Rezin, king of Syria, took Elath from the Syrians" (2 Kings 16:6).
3. The term also refers to the people of the Syrians, particularly in accounts of war or captivity: "the Syrians had come out in troops, and had carried away a little girl from the land of Israel" (2 Kings 5:2).
4. By extension, Syria also represents the pagan religious universe: Israel "served the Baals and the Ashtoreths, the gods of Syria" (Judges 10:6), showing that this territory is associated with idolatry.
H0758I.origine: The name Aram in Hebrew means "exalted" or "high." It originally refers to the Arameans, a Semitic people related to the Hebrews, who settled in this region of the Levant. This people and its territory bear the same name in the Old Testament: Aram can refer to the people, the region, or the political kingdom. The Syria of our modern maps roughly corresponds to the territory called Aram in the Bible.
H0758I.emploi: Aram appears more than 100 times in the Old Testament, especially in the books of Kings and Chronicles. The context is primarily political and military: the kings of Syria make alliances, demand gold and silver, and engage in wars against Israel and Judah for several centuries (2 Samuel 8:5; 1 Kings 20; 2 Kings 8:13). The country also appears in miracle accounts, such as the story of Naaman, the Syrian general healed of his leprosy (2 Kings 5). In a few passages, Syria is cited as an example of idolatrous power: its gods are listed among the deities that the Israelites have forsaken.
H0758I.portee: Syria reminds the reader that the faith of Israel was built amidst powerful enemies and rival religious influences. These conflicts show that the people of God had to remain faithful despite political pressure and the allure of foreign religions. The story of Naaman, healed by the God of Israel while being Syrian, illustrates that the power of God transcends borders and can touch the heart of anyone willing to turn to Him.
